questions.question: A singly linked list is maintained with a head pointer only — there is no tail pointer and no size field. What is the worst-case time to append a new node at the end of a list of n nodes?
questions.question_html: A singly linked list is maintained with a head pointer only — there is no tail pointer and no size field. What is the worst-case time to append a new node at the end of a list of n nodes?
options: Θ(log n)
Θ(n)
Θ(n log n)
questions.solution:
Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Concept. Insertion into a linked list is constant time only when the predecessor is already in hand. With a head pointer alone the last node is not addressable, so it must be found by walking.

Step by step.

  1. Start at the head and follow next until the node whose next is NULL.
  2. That walk touches all n nodes.
  3. The link assignment itself is one operation, but the search dominates: Θ(n).
  4. Keeping a tail pointer makes the same append Θ(1), because the old last node is then directly available.

Common trap. "Insertion in a linked list is O(1)" is a statement about insertion at a known position, usually the head. Without a tail pointer the position is not known.

Takeaway. A linked list buys O(1) insertion at the ends only if you keep pointers to the ends.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Binary search is run on a sorted singly linked list of n nodes. Compared with the same algorithm on a sorted array, its running time is:
questions.question_html: Binary search is run on a sorted singly linked list of n nodes. Compared with the same algorithm on a sorted array, its running time is:
options: Θ(log n)
Θ(√n)
Θ(n)
Θ(n log n)
questions.solution:
Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Concept. Each probe of binary search needs random access to the middle of the current range. An array gives that in Θ(1); a linked list gives it only after a walk from the start of the range, which costs time proportional to the range length.

Step by step.

  1. The first probe walks about n/2 nodes, the next about n/4, and so on.
  2. The recurrence is T(n) = T(n/2) + Θ(n), whose solution is Θ(n).
  3. The number of comparisons is still Θ(log n); the traversal cost is what changes the bound.
  4. So the list version is Θ(n), no better than one linear scan.

Common trap. Counting only comparisons and concluding Θ(log n). The bound must cover every operation the algorithm performs, including the ones that reach a position.

Takeaway. A good asymptotic bound counts the cost of reaching data, not just the cost of comparing it.

questions.question: The function below is called with the head of a singly linked list that holds 10 nodes and contains no cycle. What does it return? int count(struct node *h) { struct node *p = h, *q = h; int c = 0; while (p != NULL && p->next != NULL) { p = p->next->next; q = q->next; c++; } return c; }
questions.question_html:
The function below is called with the head of a singly linked list that holds 10 nodes and contains no cycle. What does it return?

int count(struct node *h) { struct node *p = h, *q = h; int c = 0; while (p != NULL && p->next != NULL) { p = p->next->next; q = q->next; c++; } return c; }
questions.solution:
Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Concept. The loop condition protects two dereferences: p must exist and p->next must exist. So the loop body runs while p is one of the first n − 1 nodes, and each iteration advances p by two nodes.

Step by step.

  1. Iteration 1: p moves from node 1 to node 3, c = 1.
  2. Iteration 2: p 3 → 5, c = 2.
  3. Iteration 3: p 5 → 7, c = 3.
  4. Iteration 4: p 7 → 9, c = 4.
  5. Iteration 5: node 9 still has a successor, so the body runs again and p becomes NULL, c = 5. The condition now fails on p != NULL.
  6. The function returns 5, which is n/2 for n = 10.

Common trap. Stopping at c = 4 by assuming the loop ends when p reaches the last node. It ends one iteration later, when p steps past it, because node 9 does have a successor.

Takeaway. Trace the guard, not the intent: p->next != NULL allows one more jump from the last node.

  5. Iteration 5: node 9 still has a successor, so the body runs again and p becomes NULL, c = 5. The condition now fails on p != NULL.

Common trap. Stopping at c = 4 by assuming the loop ends when p reaches the last node. It ends one iteration later, when p steps past it, because node 9 does have a successor.

Takeaway. Trace the guard, not the intent: p->next != NULL allows one more jump from the last node.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Which one of the following is not an application of a stack?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following is not an application of a stack?
options: Converting an infix expression to postfix
Checking whether the parentheses in an expression are balanced
Round-robin CPU scheduling
Evaluating a postfix expression
options_html: Converting an infix expression to postfix
Checking whether the parentheses in an expression are balanced
questions.solution:
Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Concept. A stack is last-in-first-out and is used wherever the most recent unfinished item must be resumed first — nested brackets, nested calls, the rightmost pending operator. Round-robin scheduling keeps processes in arrival order and resumes the oldest one, which is first-in-first-out.

Step by step.

  1. Infix to postfix: the pending operators are held on a stack and the most recent one is popped first.
  2. Bracket matching: each closing bracket must match the most recently opened one, a LIFO match.
  3. Postfix evaluation: the two most recently seen operands are consumed by each operator.
  4. Round-robin scheduling: processes leave in the order they arrived, which is a queue.

Common trap. Treating every "data structure" answer as interchangeable. The test is the order of resumption: LIFO is a stack, FIFO is a queue.

Takeaway. Ask which item must be served first; the answer names the structure.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: The postfix expression A B C + * D - is equivalent to which one of the following infix expressions?
questions.question_html: The postfix expression A B C + * D - is equivalent to which one of the following infix expressions?
options: A * B + C - D
questions.solution:
Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Concept. Postfix is read left to right; operands are pushed and an operator pops the two most recent operands, taking the second popped as its left operand. The parenthesisation is therefore fixed by the order of the operators, not by any convention about precedence.

Step by step.

  1. Push A, B, C.
  2. The first operator is +: it pops C then B, giving the subexpression (B + C).
  3. The next operator is *: it pops (B + C) then A, giving (A * (B + C)).
  4. The last operator is -: it pops D then (A * (B + C)), giving (A * (B + C)) - D.

Common trap. Reading the trailing D - as D subtracted from the whole, or as (C − D) — the second operand popped is the left operand, and D is the second operand here.

Takeaway. In postfix conversion the operator always takes the last two things on the stack, in the order they were pushed.

questions.question: Two stacks share a single array of 20 slots, indexed 0 to 19. Stack 1 grows upward from index 0 and its top is currently at index 8; stack 2 grows downward from index 19 and its top is currently at index 10. How many more pushes can be accepted before an overflow?
questions.question_html: Two stacks share a single array of 20 slots, indexed 0 to 19. Stack 1 grows upward from index 0 and its top is currently at index 8; stack 2 grows downward from index 19 and its top is currently at index 10. How many more pushes can be accepted before an overflow?
questions.solution:
Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Concept. The two stacks collide when the top of the upward stack and the top of the downward stack become adjacent. Every index strictly between the two tops is free, so the free count is top2 − top1 − 1, and the overflow test is top1 + 1 == top2.

Step by step.

  1. Stack 1 occupies indices 0 to 8; stack 2 occupies indices 10 to 19.
  2. Index 9 is the only slot that belongs to neither stack.
  3. Free slots = 10 − 8 − 1 = 1.
  4. One more push fills index 9 and the next one overflows.

Common trap. Computing 19 − 8 = 11 and forgetting that the eleven indices above stack 1 are mostly occupied by stack 2. Only the gap between the two tops is available.

Takeaway. In a shared array the capacity is the gap between the tops, not the distance from one top to the end of the array.

questions.question: The postfix expression 3 4 2 * 1 5 - 2 3 ^ ^ / + is evaluated with a stack. What is the maximum number of elements held on the stack at any instant?
questions.question_html: The postfix expression 3 4 2 * 1 5 - 2 3 ^ ^ / + is evaluated with a stack. What is the maximum number of elements held on the stack at any instant?
questions.solution:
Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Concept. While scanning postfix, a stack element is added by every operand and removed twice and replaced once by every binary operator. The peak depth therefore depends on where the operands cluster, and must be read off a trace rather than guessed from the number of operands.

Step by step.

  1. 3 → depth 1; 4 → 2; 2 → 3.
  2. * pops two and pushes one → depth 2 (stack 3, 8).
  3. 1 → 3; 5 → 4; - → 3 (stack 3, 8, −4).
  4. 2 → 4; 3 → 5 — this is the peak.
  5. The remaining operators only reduce the depth: ^ → 4, ^ → 3, / → 2, + → 1.

Common trap. Reporting 4 by forgetting that 2 and 3 are both pushed before the second ^ is applied, or counting the final single result.

Takeaway. For a peak-depth question, write the depth after every token; never estimate from the number of operators.

questions.question: Which of the following supports insertion and deletion at both ends in Θ(1) worst-case time?
questions.question_html: Which of the following supports insertion and deletion at both ends in Θ(1) worst-case time?
options: A singly linked list with a head pointer only
An array with a single front index
A doubly linked list with head and tail pointers
A binary min-heap
options_html: A singly linked list with a head pointer only
An array with a single front index
A doubly linked list with head and tail pointers
questions.solution:
Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Concept. A deque needs a handle on both ends, and every node on the end being changed must have a pointer to its inward neighbour. A doubly linked list supplies that from either side; a singly linked list does not, because a node has no way back.

Step by step.

  1. Singly linked list with head only: removal at the tail needs a full walk, Θ(n).
  2. Array with one front index: removing at the front forces a shift, Θ(n).
  3. Doubly linked list with head and tail: each end operation rewrites a constant number of pointers, Θ(1).
  4. A binary heap supports the minimum only, and its other end is not a deque end.

Common trap. Assuming a singly linked list with a tail pointer would do. A tail pointer finds the last node but cannot reach its predecessor, so tail deletion still costs a walk.

Takeaway. A double-ended structure needs backward links, not just end pointers.

questions.question: A circular array of 8 slots (indices 0 to 7) implements a queue in which one slot is always left unused. front is the index of the first element, count is the number of elements, and rear is the index of the next free slot. With front = 3 and count = 5 , what is rear ?
questions.question_html: A circular array of 8 slots (indices 0 to 7) implements a queue in which one slot is always left unused. front is the index of the first element, count is the number of elements, and rear is the index of the next free slot. With front = 3 and count = 5, what is rear?
questions.solution:
Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Concept. In a circular array every index is reduced modulo the array size. Since count elements occupy the slots front, front + 1, …, front + count − 1, the next free slot is (front + count) mod 8.

Step by step.

  1. front + count = 3 + 5 = 8.
  2. 8 mod 8 = 0.
  3. Check the occupancy: the five elements sit in slots 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, so the next free slot is 0 — the queue has wrapped exactly once.

Common trap. Answering 8, which is not an index of an array of 8 slots. The wrap is the whole point of the circular representation.

Takeaway. Reduce modulo the size before interpreting an index, never after.

questions.question: A deque is initially empty. The operations push_back(1) , push_back(2) , push_back(3) , push_back(4) , push_back(5) , pop_front() , pop_front() , push_front(6) , pop_back() , pop_back() are performed in that order. What remains, from front to back?
questions.question_html: A deque is initially empty. The operations push_back(1), push_back(2), push_back(3), push_back(4), push_back(5), pop_front(), pop_front(), push_front(6), pop_back(), pop_back() are performed in that order. What remains, from front to back?
questions.solution:
Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Concept. A deque has four distinct ends: push_front and push_back add at opposite ends, and pop_front and pop_back remove from opposite ends. Keeping the front and the back apart is the only thing the question tests.

Step by step.

  1. After the five push_back calls: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
  2. Two pop_front calls remove 1 and 2: 3, 4, 5.
  3. push_front(6) adds at the front: 6, 3, 4, 5.
  4. Two pop_back calls remove 5 and 4: 6, 3.

Common trap. Treating push_front(6) as an append, which leaves 3, 4, 5, 6 and, after two pops at the back, 3, 4.

Takeaway. Write the deque out after each operation; four ends are easy to confuse in the head.

questions.question: The lower triangle, diagonal included, of an n × n symmetric matrix is stored row by row in a one-dimensional array T with 1-based indexing, T[1] holding the element (1, 1) . Which of the following statements are TRUE?
questions.question_html: The lower triangle, diagonal included, of an n × n symmetric matrix is stored row by row in a one-dimensional array T with 1-based indexing, T[1] holding the element (1, 1). Which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: For n = 10 the array needs 55 locations.
For i ≥ j the element (i, j) is stored at T[i(i − 1)/2 + j] .
For n = 100 the array needs 5050 locations.
This packing halves the storage requirement only when n is even.
options_html: For n = 10 the array needs 55 locations.
For i ≥ j the element (i, j) is stored at T[i(i − 1)/2 + j].
For n = 100 the array needs 5050 locations.
This packing halves the storage requirement only when n is even.
questions.solution:
Answer: Options (A), (B), (C)

Detailed solution

Concept. A symmetric matrix satisfies A[i][j] = A[j][i], so the lower triangle carries all the information. Row i of the triangle holds i elements, so the total is 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2, and the element (i, j) with i ≥ j is preceded by all complete rows above it plus j − 1 elements of its own row.

Step by step.

  1. (A) TRUE. 10 × 11 / 2 = 55.
  2. (B) TRUE. Rows 1 to i − 1 hold i(i − 1)/2 elements, and (i, j) is the j-th in row i, so the 1-based position is i(i − 1)/2 + j. Check: (3, 2) gives 3 + 2 = 5, and the row layout is 1 | 2 3 | 4 5 6, so the fifth entry is indeed (3, 2).
  3. (C) TRUE. 100 × 101 / 2 = 5050.
  4. (D) FALSE. The saving is n2 − n(n + 1)/2 = n(n − 1)/2 entries for every n, and the ratio tends to one half as n grows. Parity plays no part.

Common trap. Checking only the closed-form count and forgetting to verify the index formula on an actual element, or assuming the ratio is exactly one half when it is only asymptotically one half.

Takeaway. For a packed triangular array, verify the index formula on a small element in the middle of the triangle.

questions.question: A circular doubly linked list of n nodes is maintained with a head pointer that is never NULL . Which of the following statements are TRUE?
questions.question_html: A circular doubly linked list of n nodes is maintained with a head pointer that is never NULL. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: The last node's next field points to the head node.
head->prev points to the last node.
Walking forward from the head with next pointers returns to the head after exactly n steps.
Inserting a new node immediately before the head requires rewriting exactly two link fields.
options_html: The last node's next field points to the head node.
head->prev points to the last node.
Walking forward from the head with next pointers returns to the head after exactly n steps.
Inserting a new node immediately before the head requires rewriting exactly two link fields.
questions.solution:
Answer: Options (A), (B), (C)

Detailed solution

Concept. In a circular list the ring is closed in both directions: the last node's next is the head and the head's prev is the last node. In a doubly linked structure every node is referenced from two sides, so an insertion or a deletion touches both neighbours plus the new node's own two fields.

Step by step.

  1. (A) TRUE. That link is what makes the list circular.
  2. (B) TRUE. The backward ring mirrors the forward one.
  3. (C) TRUE. Each step visits one new node, and after n steps the walk has returned to the starting node.
  4. (D) FALSE. Four fields change: new->next, new->prev, head->prev->next and head->prev.

Common trap. Counting only the two writes into the new node and forgetting the two neighbours, or thinking (C) needs n + 1 steps because the walk returns to the head "after" the last node.

Takeaway. Count fields by counting references: a doubly linked insertion touches four.

questions.question: A stack is implemented with a singly linked list in which every push inserts at the head and every pop removes the head. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
questions.question_html: A stack is implemented with a singly linked list in which every push inserts at the head and every pop removes the head. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: push runs in Θ(1) worst-case time.
pop runs in Θ(1) worst-case time.
Pushing at the tail would also run in Θ(1) without a tail pointer.
The stack can overflow only when memory is exhausted.
options_html: push runs in Θ(1) worst-case time.
pop runs in Θ(1) worst-case time.
Pushing at the tail would also run in Θ(1) without a tail pointer.
The stack can overflow only when memory is exhausted.
questions.solution:
Answer: Options (A), (B), (D)

Detailed solution

Concept. The head of a singly linked list is the only position that is directly addressable, which is exactly what a stack needs: the top must be reachable in constant time. A linked implementation has no fixed capacity, so the classical "stack overflow" of an array-backed stack becomes allocation failure.

Step by step.

  1. (A) TRUE. Inserting at the head rewrites one pointer.
  2. (B) TRUE. Removing the head rewrites one pointer and frees one node.
  3. (C) FALSE. Without a tail pointer, reaching the last node costs a walk of Θ(n).
  4. (D) TRUE. The size is limited by available memory, not by a declared capacity.

Common trap. Carrying the array's overflow notion over to a linked stack, or assuming the tail is as cheap as the head.

Takeaway. A linked stack is the head of a list; that single fact answers cost, capacity and correctness together.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: The maximum of every window of size k in an array of n values is computed with a deque that stores indices. Before each insertion, the indices at the back whose values are less than or equal to the incoming value are removed; the index at the front is removed once it has left the window. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
questions.question_html: The maximum of every window of size k in an array of n values is computed with a deque that stores indices. Before each insertion, the indices at the back whose values are less than or equal to the incoming value are removed; the index at the front is removed once it has left the window. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: The deque holds at most k indices at any time.
The values at the indices in the deque increase from front to back.
Each index enters the deque once and leaves it at most once, so the total work is Θ(n) .
The front of the deque always holds the index of the maximum of the current window.
options_html: The deque holds at most k indices at any time.
The values at the indices in the deque increase from front to back.
Each index enters the deque once and leaves it at most once, so the total work is Θ(n).
The front of the deque always holds the index of the maximum of the current window.
questions.solution:
Answer: Options (A), (C), (D)

Detailed solution

Concept. The deque keeps only the indices that can still become a window maximum: a value that is smaller and older than a later value can never be the answer again, so it is discarded at the back. What survives is a decreasing sequence of values whose indices increase — a monotone deque.

Step by step.

  1. (A) TRUE. Only indices inside the current window are retained, and the window holds k positions.
  2. (B) FALSE. The values decrease from front to back: the front is the largest. Any value greater than its predecessor would have evicted that predecessor at the back.
  3. (C) TRUE. Every index is pushed once, and each index is removed at most once, so the amortised cost per step is constant and the total is Θ(n).
  4. (D) TRUE. Discarding smaller values at the back and expired indices at the front leaves exactly the largest value of the window at the front.

Common trap. Reading the monotonicity in the wrong direction, or thinking the deque costs Θ(nk) because the removals look like extra work.

Takeaway. In an amortised structure, count how often each element can enter and leave, not how many operations one step may perform.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: A queue returns elements in the reverse of the order in which they were inserted.
A deque allows insertion and deletion at both ends.
In a circular queue, no element has to be shifted when an element is removed from the front.
A queue built on a singly linked list with both head and tail pointers enqueues in Θ(n) time.
options_html: A queue returns elements in the reverse of the order in which they were inserted.
A deque allows insertion and deletion at both ends.
In a circular queue, no element has to be shifted when an element is removed from the front.
A queue built on a singly linked list with both head and tail pointers enqueues in Θ(n) time.
questions.solution:
Answer: Options (B), (C)

Detailed solution

Concept. A queue is first-in-first-out: the element inserted earliest leaves first. A circular representation removes the shifting that a plain array would need, and a tail pointer makes the enqueue a constant-time operation.

Step by step.

  1. (A) FALSE. Reversal is the behaviour of a stack, not a queue.
  2. (B) TRUE. That is the definition of a double-ended queue.
  3. (C) TRUE. The front index simply advances modulo the array size.
  4. (D) FALSE. With a tail pointer the insertion is Θ(1).

Common trap. Confusing FIFO with LIFO in the first statement, or assuming that any linked-list operation is linear.

Takeaway. Queue means FIFO; the data structure chosen to implement it should not change that.

Step by step.

  1. (A) FALSE. Reversal is the behaviour of a stack, not a queue.
  2. (B) TRUE. That is the definition of a double-ended queue.
  3. (C) TRUE. The front index simply advances modulo the array size.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: How many elements does the array int A[-2..5][3..7][1..4]; hold?
questions.question_html: How many elements does the array int A[-2..5][3..7][1..4]; hold?
questions.solution:
Answer: 160

Detailed solution

Concept. The number of values along one dimension is upper − lower + 1, and the total is the product of the three counts. Negative lower bounds are allowed and change only the count, not the address formula.

Step by step.

  1. First dimension: 5 − (−2) + 1 = 8.
  2. Second dimension: 7 − 3 + 1 = 5.
  3. Third dimension: 4 − 1 + 1 = 4.
  4. Total = 8 × 5 × 4 = 160.

Common trap. Using the upper bounds themselves as counts, 5 × 7 × 4 = 140, or 7 × 4 × 3 = 84 by dropping the negative sign.

Takeaway. Count per dimension with the +1, then multiply.

questions.question: A circular singly linked list has 12 nodes, and each node stores only data and next . You are given a pointer p to one node, but not the head. What is the minimum number of next -pointer steps needed to reach the node whose next field points to p ?
questions.question_html: A circular singly linked list has 12 nodes, and each node stores only data and next. You are given a pointer p to one node, but not the head. What is the minimum number of next-pointer steps needed to reach the node whose next field points to p?
questions.solution:
Answer: 11

Detailed solution

Concept. In a circular list every node is reachable from every other node by following next. The predecessor of p is the last distinct node on the way round, so it is reached after n − 1 steps, and no shorter walk exists because a singly linked list cannot go backwards.

Step by step.

  1. Start at p, which is step 0.
  2. Following next visits the 11 other nodes in turn.
  3. The eleventh distinct node visited has next == p, so it is the predecessor.
  4. Answer: 11 steps.

Common trap. Answering 12 by counting the return to p itself, which is one step beyond the predecessor.

Takeaway. On a ring of n nodes the predecessor of a node is n − 1 steps ahead, and the node itself is n steps ahead.

questions.question: The infix expression A - B + C * (D - E) + F is converted to postfix with the standard operator-stack algorithm. Counting only operators that are popped from the stack — the parenthesis that is discarded on ) is not counted — how many pops occur in total, including the flush of the stack at the end?
questions.question_html: The infix expression A - B + C * (D - E) + F is converted to postfix with the standard operator-stack algorithm. Counting only operators that are popped from the stack — the parenthesis that is discarded on ) is not counted — how many pops occur in total, including the flush of the stack at the end?
questions.solution:
Answer: 5

Detailed solution

Concept. The algorithm pops while the operator on top of the stack has precedence greater than or equal to the incoming operator, and pops everything down to the matching ( when a ) arrives. Equal precedence pops too, because subtraction and addition are left-associative.

Step by step.

  1. - is pushed; on + the top - has equal precedence, so it is popped (1).
  2. * is pushed above +; ( is pushed; - is pushed inside the bracket.
  3. On ) the inner - is popped (2); the ( is then discarded and is not an operator.
  4. On the second +: * is popped (3) and then + is popped (4).
  5. At the end the remaining + is popped (5). Total 5.

Common trap. Forgetting the flush at the end (giving 4), or forgetting that equal precedence pops, so that the first + leaves the - on the stack (giving 3).

Takeaway. Trace the stack token by token, and remember that left-associative operators pop their equals.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: The integers 1, 2, 3, 4 are pushed onto an initially empty stack in that order, each exactly once, and elements may be popped at any time, including between pushes. How many different output sequences can be produced?
questions.question_html: The integers 1, 2, 3, 4 are pushed onto an initially empty stack in that order, each exactly once, and elements may be popped at any time, including between pushes. How many different output sequences can be produced?
questions.solution:
Answer: 14

Detailed solution

Concept. The number of distinct permutations of 1 … n obtainable from a single stack with a fixed input order is the n-th Catalan number Cn = (1/(n+1)) × binom(2n, n). Each push/pop schedule corresponds to a balanced parenthesis string of length 2n.

Step by step.

  1. For n = 4: binom(8, 4) = 70.
  2. Divide by n + 1 = 5: 70 / 5 = 14.
  3. Sanity check by enumeration: starting from 1 and repeatedly either pushing the next integer or popping, exactly 14 distinct output orders arise; for example 4, 3, 2, 1 is possible and 4, 1, 2, 3 is not.

Common trap. Answering 4! = 24 by assuming every permutation is reachable, or 23 = 8 by counting the choice points instead of the outcomes. Permutations such as 3, 1, 2, 4 are impossible.

Takeaway. Stack-ordered permutations are counted by Catalan numbers, not by factorials.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A queue is built from two stacks S1 and S2 . Enqueue pushes onto S1 . Dequeue pops from S2 , and only when S2 is empty is every element of S1 popped and pushed onto S2 before the pop. Starting from empty, the operations are: enqueue 1, enqueue 2, enqueue 3, dequeue, enqueue 4, dequeue, dequeue. How many elements remain in the queue afterwards?
questions.question_html: A queue is built from two stacks S1 and S2. Enqueue pushes onto S1. Dequeue pops from S2, and only when S2 is empty is every element of S1 popped and pushed onto S2 before the pop. Starting from empty, the operations are: enqueue 1, enqueue 2, enqueue 3, dequeue, enqueue 4, dequeue, dequeue. How many elements remain in the queue afterwards?
questions.solution:
Answer: 1

Detailed solution

Concept. The transfer of S1 into S2 reverses the order twice — once going in and once coming out — which is exactly the FIFO behaviour a queue needs. The elements are split between the two stacks at any moment, so the queue's size is |S1| + |S2|.

Step by step.

  1. Enqueue 1, 2, 3: S1 = [1, 2, 3] with 3 on top, S2 empty.
  2. Dequeue: transfer gives S2 = [3, 2, 1] with 1 on top, then pop returns 1. S2 = [3, 2].
  3. Enqueue 4: S1 = [4].
  4. Dequeue returns 2 from S2; dequeue returns 3. S2 is now empty.
  5. Remaining: S1 = [4], so 1 element.

Common trap. Forgetting that enqueue goes to S1 while S2 still holds elements, which leads to counting 2, or assuming the transfer happens on every dequeue.

Takeaway. Track both stacks separately; the queue is their union, and the transfer happens only when S2 is empty.

questions.question: In a binary tree the height of a node is the number of edges on the longest downward path from that node to a leaf, and the height of the tree is the height of the root. What are the minimum and the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height 5?
questions.question_html: In a binary tree the height of a node is the number of edges on the longest downward path from that node to a leaf, and the height of the tree is the height of the root. What are the minimum and the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height 5?
options: 6 and 63
5 and 63
6 and 32
7 and 64
questions.solution: Concept. A binary tree of height h spans levels 0 to h, that is h + 1 levels. The fewest nodes come from a single chain, the most from a perfect tree in which every level is completely filled.Step by step.Minimum: one node per level, so h + 1 = 6 nodes.Maximum: level i holds at most 2^i nodes, so the total is 2^0 + 2^1 + … + 2^5 = 2^6 − 1 = 63.The pair is therefore 6 and 63.Answer: Option (A) — 6 and 63Common trap. Using 2^h − 1 = 31 or 2^h = 32 for the maximum, which counts levels 1 to h and drops level 0, or giving 5 as the minimum by treating the height as the number of levels.Takeaway. Height counted in edges means h + 1 levels, so the maximum is always 2^(h+1) − 1.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. A binary tree of height h spans levels 0 to h, that is h + 1 levels. The fewest nodes come from a single chain, the most from a perfect tree in which every level is completely filled.

Step by step.

  1. Minimum: one node per level, so h + 1 = 6 nodes.
  2. Maximum: level i holds at most 2^i nodes, so the total is 2^0 + 2^1 + … + 2^5 = 2^6 − 1 = 63.
  3. The pair is therefore 6 and 63.

Answer: Option (A) — 6 and 63

Common trap. Using 2^h − 1 = 31 or 2^h = 32 for the maximum, which counts levels 1 to h and drops level 0, or giving 5 as the minimum by treating the height as the number of levels.

Takeaway. Height counted in edges means h + 1 levels, so the maximum is always 2^(h+1) − 1.

questions.question: A complete binary tree has 15 nodes. The root is at level 0 and the height is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. What is the height of this tree?
questions.question_html: A complete binary tree has 15 nodes. The root is at level 0 and the height is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. What is the height of this tree?
questions.solution: Concept. In a complete binary tree every level except possibly the last is full, and the last level is filled from the left. So the node count of a complete tree of height h lies between 2^h and 2^(h+1) − 1.Step by step.Levels 0 to 2 can hold at most 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 nodes, which is fewer than 15.Levels 0 to 3 can hold at most 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 nodes, exactly 15.So the tree is the perfect tree with four complete levels and its height is 3.Answer: Option (D) — 3Common trap. Answering 4 by counting the levels 0, 1, 2, 3 instead of the edges, or answering 7 by taking log2 15 rounded up as the height.Takeaway. n nodes in a complete tree give height ⌊log2 n⌋ = 3 when the count is exactly 2^(h+1) − 1.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. In a complete binary tree every level except possibly the last is full, and the last level is filled from the left. So the node count of a complete tree of height h lies between 2^h and 2^(h+1) − 1.

Step by step.

  1. Levels 0 to 2 can hold at most 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 nodes, which is fewer than 15.
  2. Levels 0 to 3 can hold at most 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 nodes, exactly 15.
  3. So the tree is the perfect tree with four complete levels and its height is 3.

Answer: Option (D) — 3

Common trap. Answering 4 by counting the levels 0, 1, 2, 3 instead of the edges, or answering 7 by taking log2 15 rounded up as the height.

Takeaway. n nodes in a complete tree give height ⌊log2 n⌋ = 3 when the count is exactly 2^(h+1) − 1.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A full binary tree is one in which every node has either 0 or 2 children. If such a tree has 41 leaves, how many nodes does it have in total?
questions.question_html: A full binary tree is one in which every node has either 0 or 2 children. If such a tree has 41 leaves, how many nodes does it have in total?
questions.solution: Concept. In a full (proper) binary tree the number of leaves and the number of internal nodes differ by exactly one: L = I + 1.Step by step.With L = 41, the internal nodes are I = L − 1 = 40.Total nodes n = L + I = 41 + 40 = 81.Equivalently n = 2L − 1 = 81.Answer: 81Common trap. Reporting 82 by using 2L, or 40 by answering with the number of internal nodes instead of the total.Takeaway. Full tree: L = I + 1 and n = 2L − 1. Both follow from counting edges two ways.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. In a full (proper) binary tree the number of leaves and the number of internal nodes differ by exactly one: L = I + 1.

Step by step.

  1. With L = 41, the internal nodes are I = L − 1 = 40.
  2. Total nodes n = L + I = 41 + 40 = 81.
  3. Equivalently n = 2L − 1 = 81.

Answer: 81

Common trap. Reporting 82 by using 2L, or 40 by answering with the number of internal nodes instead of the total.

Takeaway. Full tree: L = I + 1 and n = 2L − 1. Both follow from counting edges two ways.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A complete binary tree with 100 nodes is stored in a 1-indexed array A[1..100]: the root is A[1], and the children of the node at index i are at 2i and 2i + 1. How many of the 100 array cells hold leaves?
questions.question_html: A complete binary tree with 100 nodes is stored in a 1-indexed array A[1..100]: the root is A[1], and the children of the node at index i are at 2i and 2i + 1. How many of the 100 array cells hold leaves?
questions.solution: Concept. In the array form of a complete binary tree the internal nodes occupy the first ⌊n/2⌋ cells, because a node has a child exactly when 2i ≤ n.Step by step.Internal nodes: ⌊100/2⌋ = 50, occupying A[1] to A[50].Leaves: 100 − 50 = 50, occupying A[51] to A[100].Check: A[50] has children A[100] and A[101], and only the first exists, so the boundary is right.Answer: Option (A) — 50Common trap. Reporting 49 by assuming a node needs both children to count as internal, or 51 by rounding the half upwards.Takeaway. Leaves = ⌈n/2⌉ and internal nodes = ⌊n/2⌋ for any complete binary tree.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. In the array form of a complete binary tree the internal nodes occupy the first ⌊n/2⌋ cells, because a node has a child exactly when 2i ≤ n.

Step by step.

  1. Internal nodes: ⌊100/2⌋ = 50, occupying A[1] to A[50].
  2. Leaves: 100 − 50 = 50, occupying A[51] to A[100].
  3. Check: A[50] has children A[100] and A[101], and only the first exists, so the boundary is right.

Answer: Option (A) — 50

Common trap. Reporting 49 by assuming a node needs both children to count as internal, or 51 by rounding the half upwards.

Takeaway. Leaves = ⌈n/2⌉ and internal nodes = ⌊n/2⌋ for any complete binary tree.

questions.question: For a non-empty binary tree let n be the number of nodes, n0 the number of leaves, n1 the number of nodes with exactly one child, n2 the number with two children, and h the height in edges. Which of the following are always TRUE?
questions.question_html: For a non-empty binary tree let n be the number of nodes, n0 the number of leaves, n1 the number of nodes with exactly one child, n2 the number with two children, and h the height in edges. Which of the following are always TRUE?
options: n = n0 + n1 + n2
Every level i (root at level 0) holds exactly 2^i nodes.
options_html: Every level i (root at level 0) holds exactly 2^i nodes.
questions.solution: Concept. The first two identities come from counting the nodes and then the edges of the same tree two different ways; the height bound comes from the largest tree a given height can hold.Step by step.(B) Every node falls in exactly one class, so n = n0 + n1 + n2.A tree with n nodes has n − 1 edges. Counting edges by parent type gives n1 + 2n2, hence n − 1 = n1 + 2n2.Substituting (B) into that equation gives n0 + n1 + n2 − 1 = n1 + 2n2, so n0 = n2 + 1: (A) holds.A tree of height h holds at most 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes, so n ≤ 2^(h+1) − 1, giving h ≥ log2(n + 1) − 1 and, since h is an integer, h ≥ ⌈log2(n + 1)⌉ − 1: (C) holds.(D) fails for a chain: it has one node per level, not 2^i.Answer: Options (A), (B), (C)Common trap. Accepting (D) because it is true for a perfect tree and forgetting that a general binary tree may leave levels half empty.Takeaway. n0 = n2 + 1 holds for every binary tree, not only for full ones.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The first two identities come from counting the nodes and then the edges of the same tree two different ways; the height bound comes from the largest tree a given height can hold.

Step by step.

  1. (B) Every node falls in exactly one class, so n = n0 + n1 + n2.
  2. A tree with n nodes has n − 1 edges. Counting edges by parent type gives n1 + 2n2, hence n − 1 = n1 + 2n2.
  3. Substituting (B) into that equation gives n0 + n1 + n2 − 1 = n1 + 2n2, so n0 = n2 + 1: (A) holds.
  4. A tree of height h holds at most 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes, so n ≤ 2^(h+1) − 1, giving h ≥ log2(n + 1) − 1 and, since h is an integer, h ≥ ⌈log2(n + 1)⌉ − 1: (C) holds.
  5. (D) fails for a chain: it has one node per level, not 2^i.

Answer: Options (A), (B), (C)

Common trap. Accepting (D) because it is true for a perfect tree and forgetting that a general binary tree may leave levels half empty.

Takeaway. n0 = n2 + 1 holds for every binary tree, not only for full ones.

questions.question: How many structurally different binary trees with exactly 5 nodes are there, where a left child and a right child are treated as different?
questions.question_html: How many structurally different binary trees with exactly 5 nodes are there, where a left child and a right child are treated as different?
questions.solution: Concept. Ordered binary tree shapes with n nodes are counted by the Catalan numbers C_n = C(2n, n)/(n + 1).Step by step.The first Catalan numbers are C_0 = 1, C_1 = 1, C_2 = 2, C_3 = 5, C_4 = 14, C_5 = 42.With n = 5: C(10, 5) = 252 and 252 / 6 = 42.Answer: Option (B) — 42Common trap. Giving 14, which is the count for 4 nodes, or 120 = 5!, which counts label orders rather than shapes.Takeaway. Shapes with n nodes: Catalan C_n; labelled trees are a different, larger count.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Ordered binary tree shapes with n nodes are counted by the Catalan numbers C_n = C(2n, n)/(n + 1).

Step by step.

  1. The first Catalan numbers are C_0 = 1, C_1 = 1, C_2 = 2, C_3 = 5, C_4 = 14, C_5 = 42.
  2. With n = 5: C(10, 5) = 252 and 252 / 6 = 42.

Answer: Option (B) — 42

Common trap. Giving 14, which is the count for 4 nodes, or 120 = 5!, which counts label orders rather than shapes.

Takeaway. Shapes with n nodes: Catalan C_n; labelled trees are a different, larger count.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Each node of a binary tree is stored in a record with three pointer fields: left, right and parent. For a tree with n ≥ 1 nodes, how many of the 3n pointer fields are NULL?
questions.question_html: Each node of a binary tree is stored in a record with three pointer fields: left, right and parent. For a tree with n ≥ 1 nodes, how many of the 3n pointer fields are NULL?
questions.solution: Concept. Count the NULLs field by field. Every node except the root is somebody's child, so the child pointers that are set number exactly n − 1 out of 2n. The parent pointer is set for every node except the root.Step by step.Left and right fields together: 2n fields, of which n − 1 point at a child (each edge is stored once), so 2n − (n − 1) = n + 1 are NULL.Parent fields: n fields, of which n − 1 are set, so exactly 1 (the root's) is NULL.Total NULLs (n + 1) + 1 = n + 2.Check on a single node: n = 1 gives 3 NULLs, and 1 + 2 = 3 agrees.Answer: Option (D) — n + 2Common trap. Answering n + 1 by quoting the familiar result for the two child fields and forgetting that the parent field of the root is also NULL.Takeaway. n + 1 NULLs is a statement about child links only; add one more per extra upward link.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Count the NULLs field by field. Every node except the root is somebody's child, so the child pointers that are set number exactly n − 1 out of 2n. The parent pointer is set for every node except the root.

Step by step.

  1. Left and right fields together: 2n fields, of which n − 1 point at a child (each edge is stored once), so 2n − (n − 1) = n + 1 are NULL.
  2. Parent fields: n fields, of which n − 1 are set, so exactly 1 (the root's) is NULL.
  3. Total NULLs (n + 1) + 1 = n + 2.
  4. Check on a single node: n = 1 gives 3 NULLs, and 1 + 2 = 3 agrees.

Answer: Option (D) — n + 2

Common trap. Answering n + 1 by quoting the familiar result for the two child fields and forgetting that the parent field of the root is also NULL.

Takeaway. n + 1 NULLs is a statement about child links only; add one more per extra upward link.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A binary tree with distinct keys has preorder A B D E C F and inorder D B E A C F. What is its postorder traversal?
questions.question_html: A binary tree with distinct keys has preorder A B D E C F and inorder D B E A C F. What is its postorder traversal?
options: D E B F C A
D E B C F A
E D B F C A
D B E F C A
options_html: D E B F C A
D E B C F A
E D B F C A
D B E F C A
questions.solution: Concept. The first key of the preorder is the root; its position in the inorder splits the remaining keys into the left and the right subtree.Step by step.Root is A. Inorder D B E | A | C F gives left {D, B, E} and right {C, F}.Left subtree: preorder B D E makes B the root; inorder D B E puts D on the left and E on the right.Right subtree: preorder C F makes C the root; inorder C F puts F on the right, so C has no left child.Postorder = left, right, root: D E B, then F C, then A.Answer: Option (A) — D E B F C ACommon trap. Option (B) reverses the last two keys by placing C before F, which happens if the right subtree is read as a left chain.Takeaway. Rebuild the shape from preorder plus inorder first, then read off the postorder; never try to transform the strings directly.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The first key of the preorder is the root; its position in the inorder splits the remaining keys into the left and the right subtree.

Step by step.

  1. Root is A. Inorder D B E | A | C F gives left {D, B, E} and right {C, F}.
  2. Left subtree: preorder B D E makes B the root; inorder D B E puts D on the left and E on the right.
  3. Right subtree: preorder C F makes C the root; inorder C F puts F on the right, so C has no left child.
  4. Postorder = left, right, root: D E B, then F C, then A.

Answer: Option (A) — D E B F C A

Common trap. Option (B) reverses the last two keys by placing C before F, which happens if the right subtree is read as a left chain.

Takeaway. Rebuild the shape from preorder plus inorder first, then read off the postorder; never try to transform the strings directly.

questions.question: A binary tree with 7 nodes has level-order traversal A B C D E F G and inorder traversal D B E A F C G. What is its preorder traversal?
questions.question_html: A binary tree with 7 nodes has level-order traversal A B C D E F G and inorder traversal D B E A F C G. What is its preorder traversal?
options: A B C D E F G

A B D E C F G
A B D E F C G
options_html: A B C D E F G
A D B E C F G
A B D E C F G
A B D E F C G

Level order fixes the parent-child relation level by level, and the inorder then fixes which child sits on which side.Step by step.Level order starts with A, so A is the root, and the next level is B and C, its two children.Next level D E F G: D, E are the children of B and F, G the children of C.Inorder D B E | A | F C G confirms the sides: B has D left and E right; C has F left and G right.Preorder = root, left, right: A B D E C F G.Answer: Option (C) — A B D E C F GCommon trap. Option (A) simply repeats the level order, and option (D) drops C behind E by treating the right subtree as part of the left one.Takeaway.
