questions.solution_html:
Concept. Level order fixes the parent-child relation level by level, and the inorder then fixes which child sits on which side.

Step by step.

  1. Level order starts with A, so A is the root, and the next level is B and C, its two children.
  2. Next level D E F G: D, E are the children of B and F, G the children of C.
  3. Inorder D B E | A | F C G confirms the sides: B has D left and E right; C has F left and G right.
  4. Preorder = root, left, right: A B D E C F G.

Answer: Option (C) — A B D E C F G

Common trap. Option (A) simply repeats the level order, and option (D) drops C behind E by treating the right subtree as part of the left one.

Takeaway. Level order plus inorder is enough; the level order gives the shape, the inorder the orientation.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A binary tree with the distinct keys A, B, C has preorder A B C and postorder C B A. Left and right children are distinguished. How many different binary trees satisfy both traversals together?
questions.question_html: A binary tree with the distinct keys A, B, C has preorder A B C and postorder C B A. Left and right children are distinguished. How many different binary trees satisfy both traversals together?
questions.solution: Concept. Preorder and postorder together do not determine a binary tree whenever some node has a single child: the two traversals say which node is whose child, but not on which side.Step by step.Preorder A B C forces A to be the root, B a child of A and C a child of B.Any such chain has postorder C B A whatever the sides, because each node is visited after its only child.B may be a left or a right child of A: 2 choices. C may be a left or a right child of B: 2 choices.Total 2 × 2 = 4 trees: A→B→C as left-left, left-right, right-left and right-right chains.Answer: 4Common trap. Answering 1, assuming two traversals always pin the tree down; that is true only when no node has exactly one child.Takeaway. The pair (preorder, postorder) is unique exactly when every internal node has two children.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Preorder and postorder together do not determine a binary tree whenever some node has a single child: the two traversals say which node is whose child, but not on which side.

Step by step.

  1. Preorder A B C forces A to be the root, B a child of A and C a child of B.
  2. Any such chain has postorder C B A whatever the sides, because each node is visited after its only child.
  3. B may be a left or a right child of A: 2 choices. C may be a left or a right child of B: 2 choices.
  4. Total 2 × 2 = 4 trees: A→B→C as left-left, left-right, right-left and right-right chains.

Answer: 4

Common trap. Answering 1, assuming two traversals always pin the tree down; that is true only when no node has exactly one child.

Takeaway. The pair (preorder, postorder) is unique exactly when every internal node has two children.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A binary search tree holds distinct integer keys. Which traversal lists the keys in increasing order?
questions.question_html: A binary search tree holds distinct integer keys. Which traversal lists the keys in increasing order?
options: preorder
postorder
level order
inorder
questions.solution: Concept. In a BST every key in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every key in the right subtree is larger. Inorder visits left subtree, then node, then right subtree.Step by step.Inorder emits the whole left subtree first, and by induction it is ascending and every key in it is below the node.Then the node, then the right subtree, which is ascending and entirely above the node.The concatenation is therefore ascending. Preorder and postorder visit the node before or between the subtrees, so they interleave large and small keys.Answer: Option (D) — inorderCommon trap. Choosing preorder because it starts at the root and looks ordered; the root of a BST is only the middle key, not the smallest.Takeaway. Inorder of a BST is sorted, which is why "is this tree a BST?" is answered by one inorder scan.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. In a BST every key in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every key in the right subtree is larger. Inorder visits left subtree, then node, then right subtree.

Step by step.

  1. Inorder emits the whole left subtree first, and by induction it is ascending and every key in it is below the node.
  2. Then the node, then the right subtree, which is ascending and entirely above the node.
  3. The concatenation is therefore ascending. Preorder and postorder visit the node before or between the subtrees, so they interleave large and small keys.

Answer: Option (D) — inorder

Common trap. Choosing preorder because it starts at the root and looks ordered; the root of a BST is only the middle key, not the smallest.

Takeaway. Inorder of a BST is sorted, which is why "is this tree a BST?" is answered by one inorder scan.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: For a binary tree whose keys are all distinct, which of these pairs of traversals determine the tree uniquely?
questions.question_html: For a binary tree whose keys are all distinct, which of these pairs of traversals determine the tree uniquely?
options: preorder and inorder
postorder and inorder
preorder and postorder
level order and inorder
questions.solution: Concept. A reconstruction needs one traversal that identifies the root of each subtree and one that says how the remaining keys split into left and right.Step by step.Inorder always supplies the split, because the root's position separates left keys from right keys.Preorder gives the root first, postorder gives it last, and level order gives it first within each subtree. Each of them therefore pairs with inorder: (A), (B) and (D) are unique.(C) fails: with preorder A B C and postorder C B A both the left chain and the right chain fit, so the side of a single child is unknown.Answer: Options (A), (B), (D)Common trap. Believing preorder plus postorder is enough because together they name every node in two orders; they still leave single-child nodes unoriented.Takeaway. Any traversal that names the root, plus inorder, is sufficient; two root-naming traversals without inorder are not.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. A reconstruction needs one traversal that identifies the root of each subtree and one that says how the remaining keys split into left and right.

Step by step.

  1. Inorder always supplies the split, because the root's position separates left keys from right keys.
  2. Preorder gives the root first, postorder gives it last, and level order gives it first within each subtree. Each of them therefore pairs with inorder: (A), (B) and (D) are unique.
  3. (C) fails: with preorder A B C and postorder C B A both the left chain and the right chain fit, so the side of a single child is unknown.

Answer: Options (A), (B), (D)

Common trap. Believing preorder plus postorder is enough because together they name every node in two orders; they still leave single-child nodes unoriented.

Takeaway. Any traversal that names the root, plus inorder, is sufficient; two root-naming traversals without inorder are not.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A binary tree with 9 nodes has preorder A B D G H C E F I and inorder G D H B A E C I F. How many nodes of this tree have exactly one child?
questions.question_html: A binary tree with 9 nodes has preorder A B D G H C E F I and inorder G D H B A E C I F. How many nodes of this tree have exactly one child?
questions.solution: Concept. Rebuild the tree recursively: the preorder supplies each subtree root, and the inorder says how many keys fall to its left and to its right.Step by step.Root A; inorder G D H B | A | E C I F gives 4 keys left and 4 right.Left: preorder B D G H makes B the root; inorder G D H B puts all three keys on its left, so B has no right child.Inside that left part, preorder D G H makes D the root with G left and H right.Right: preorder C E F I makes C the root; inorder E C I F gives E left and I F right, so C has two children.Preorder F I with inorder I F makes F the root with I on its left only.Single-child nodes: B (left only) and F (left only). All others have 0 or 2.Answer: Option (C) — 2Common trap. Counting the leaves G, H, E, I as single-child nodes, or stopping after the first level and answering 0.Takeaway. Draw the tree first; every later question about it (child counts, height, mirror, diameter) then becomes a lookup.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Rebuild the tree recursively: the preorder supplies each subtree root, and the inorder says how many keys fall to its left and to its right.

Step by step.

  1. Root A; inorder G D H B | A | E C I F gives 4 keys left and 4 right.
  2. Left: preorder B D G H makes B the root; inorder G D H B puts all three keys on its left, so B has no right child.
  3. Inside that left part, preorder D G H makes D the root with G left and H right.
  4. Right: preorder C E F I makes C the root; inorder E C I F gives E left and I F right, so C has two children.
  5. Preorder F I with inorder I F makes F the root with I on its left only.
  6. Single-child nodes: B (left only) and F (left only). All others have 0 or 2.

Answer: Option (C) — 2

Common trap. Counting the leaves G, H, E, I as single-child nodes, or stopping after the first level and answering 0.

Takeaway. Draw the tree first; every later question about it (child counts, height, mirror, diameter) then becomes a lookup.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: In an inorder-threaded binary tree, the right pointer of a node that has no right child is replaced by a thread. What does that thread point to?
questions.question_html: In an inorder-threaded binary tree, the right pointer of a node that has no right child is replaced by a thread. What does that thread point to?
options: its parent
its inorder successor
its inorder predecessor
the root of the tree
questions.solution: Concept. Threading reuses the NULL pointers of a binary tree to store the inorder neighbours of a node, so that inorder traversal needs no stack.Step by step.A node with no right child is the last node visited in its own subtree, so the next node of the inorder walk is its ancestor on the first turn to the right.That ancestor is the inorder successor, so the right thread points there.Symmetrically, a NULL left pointer becomes a thread to the inorder predecessor.Answer: Option (B) — its inorder successorCommon trap. Saying the parent: for a node that is a left child the successor is the parent, but for a right child it is some higher ancestor, so "parent" is not general.Takeaway. Right thread = successor, left thread = predecessor; that is what makes "find next in inorder" an O(1) step.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Threading reuses the NULL pointers of a binary tree to store the inorder neighbours of a node, so that inorder traversal needs no stack.

Step by step.

  1. A node with no right child is the last node visited in its own subtree, so the next node of the inorder walk is its ancestor on the first turn to the right.
  2. That ancestor is the inorder successor, so the right thread points there.
  3. Symmetrically, a NULL left pointer becomes a thread to the inorder predecessor.

Answer: Option (B) — its inorder successor

Common trap. Saying the parent: for a node that is a left child the successor is the parent, but for a right child it is some higher ancestor, so "parent" is not general.

Takeaway. Right thread = successor, left thread = predecessor; that is what makes "find next in inorder" an O(1) step.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A binary tree with 20 nodes is stored as a fully threaded binary tree, so every NULL left or right pointer is replaced by a thread. How many thread pointers does the tree contain?
questions.question_html: A binary tree with 20 nodes is stored as a fully threaded binary tree, so every NULL left or right pointer is replaced by a thread. How many thread pointers does the tree contain?
questions.solution: Concept. A binary tree with n nodes has exactly n + 1 NULL child pointers, because it has 2n child fields and n − 1 of them hold edges.Step by step.Child fields: 2 × 20 = 40.Fields holding a real child: 20 − 1 = 19 edges.NULL fields: 40 − 19 = 21. Full threading turns every one of them into a thread, so there are 21 threads.Answer: 21Common trap. Answering 20, one thread per node; the count is per NULL pointer, and a leaf contributes two.Takeaway. Threads = n + 1 for a fully threaded tree of n nodes, the same count as the NULL pointers it replaces.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. A binary tree with n nodes has exactly n + 1 NULL child pointers, because it has 2n child fields and n − 1 of them hold edges.

Step by step.

  1. Child fields: 2 × 20 = 40.
  2. Fields holding a real child: 20 − 1 = 19 edges.
  3. NULL fields: 40 − 19 = 21. Full threading turns every one of them into a thread, so there are 21 threads.

Answer: 21

Common trap. Answering 20, one thread per node; the count is per NULL pointer, and a leaf contributes two.

Takeaway. Threads = n + 1 for a fully threaded tree of n nodes, the same count as the NULL pointers it replaces.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Compared with an ordinary binary tree, what is the main cost of threading?
questions.question_html: Compared with an ordinary binary tree, what is the main cost of threading?
options: Each node needs an extra child pointer.
Insertion and deletion must update the threads of neighbouring nodes.
Inorder traversal needs an auxiliary stack.
The tree can no longer be searched in time proportional to its height.
options_html: Each node needs an extra child pointer.
Insertion and deletion must update the threads of neighbouring nodes.
Inorder traversal needs an auxiliary stack.
The tree can no longer be searched in time proportional to its height.
questions.solution: Concept. Threading trades update work for traversal work: it stores inorder neighbours in the unused pointers, which removes the stack but makes structural updates more delicate.Step by step.Traversal gets cheaper: inorder runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, so (C) is false.No pointer is added; a NULL child pointer is reused, possibly with one tag bit, so (A) is false.Searching still follows one path of length at most the height, so (D) is false.When a node is inserted or deleted, the threads that pointed to the old neighbour must be redirected, and that repair work is what threading costs: (B) is true.Answer: Option (B)Common trap. Assuming threading needs extra storage per node; the whole point is to reuse the NULL pointers that already exist.Takeaway. Threading pays off when the tree is built once and traversed many times.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Threading trades update work for traversal work: it stores inorder neighbours in the unused pointers, which removes the stack but makes structural updates more delicate.

Step by step.

  1. Traversal gets cheaper: inorder runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, so (C) is false.
  2. No pointer is added; a NULL child pointer is reused, possibly with one tag bit, so (A) is false.
  3. Searching still follows one path of length at most the height, so (D) is false.
  4. When a node is inserted or deleted, the threads that pointed to the old neighbour must be redirected, and that repair work is what threading costs: (B) is true.

Answer: Option (B)

Common trap. Assuming threading needs extra storage per node; the whole point is to reuse the NULL pointers that already exist.

Takeaway. Threading pays off when the tree is built once and traversed many times.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Which of the following statements about threaded binary trees are TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about threaded binary trees are TRUE?
options: In a fully threaded binary tree a NULL left pointer is replaced by a thread to the inorder predecessor.
Threading reduces the number of nodes that must be stored.
Threads must be distinguishable from ordinary child pointers, typically by a one-bit tag per pointer.
An inorder traversal of a fully threaded tree needs O(1) extra space.
options_html: In a fully threaded binary tree a NULL left pointer is replaced by a thread to the inorder predecessor.
Threading reduces the number of nodes that must be stored.
Threads must be distinguishable from ordinary child pointers, typically by a one-bit tag per pointer.
An inorder traversal of a fully threaded tree needs O(1) extra space.
questions.solution: Concept. A thread is a pointer to an inorder neighbour stored in a child field that would otherwise be NULL; a tag bit tells the two uses of the same field apart.Step by step.(A) true: the left thread of a node is its inorder predecessor, the right thread its successor.(B) false: threading changes no node count. It adds no node and removes none; only the meaning of some pointer fields changes.(C) true: without a tag the traversal cannot tell whether a field holds a child or a thread.(D) true: the successor is reached by following one thread, so no stack and no recursion is needed.Answer: Options (A), (C), (D)Common trap. Accepting (B) because threading "saves space": it saves the O(h) stack of a recursive traversal, not any node.Takeaway. Threading is a space-for-update trade inside the existing nodes.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. A thread is a pointer to an inorder neighbour stored in a child field that would otherwise be NULL; a tag bit tells the two uses of the same field apart.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true: the left thread of a node is its inorder predecessor, the right thread its successor.
  2. (B) false: threading changes no node count. It adds no node and removes none; only the meaning of some pointer fields changes.
  3. (C) true: without a tag the traversal cannot tell whether a field holds a child or a thread.
  4. (D) true: the successor is reached by following one thread, so no stack and no recursion is needed.

Answer: Options (A), (C), (D)

Common trap. Accepting (B) because threading "saves space": it saves the O(h) stack of a recursive traversal, not any node.

Takeaway. Threading is a space-for-update trade inside the existing nodes.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A fully threaded binary tree uses a dummy header node. Its left pointer points to the root, its right pointer points to itself, and it acts as the inorder predecessor of the leftmost node and the inorder successor of the rightmost node. For a tree with n ≥ 1 real nodes, how many thread pointers point at the header?
questions.question_html: A fully threaded binary tree uses a dummy header node. Its left pointer points to the root, its right pointer points to itself, and it acts as the inorder predecessor of the leftmost node and the inorder successor of the rightmost node. For a tree with n ≥ 1 real nodes, how many thread pointers point at the header?
options: n
questions.solution: Concept. With a header the structure has n + 1 nodes and therefore n + 2 threads. Every thread points at an inorder neighbour, and the header is the neighbour of exactly two nodes.Step by step.The leftmost node has no left child, so its left thread points to its inorder predecessor, which is the header.The rightmost node has no right child, so its right thread points to its inorder successor, which is again the header.Every other thread points at a real node, so exactly 2 threads reach the header.Check the count: n + 2 threads in all, of which 2 go to the header and n to real nodes.Answer: Option (C) — 2Common trap. Answering 1 by thinking only the rightmost node needs the header, or n by counting one header pointer per node.Takeaway. The header closes the inorder walk into a cycle, so the traversal can stop on returning to it instead of testing for NULL.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. With a header the structure has n + 1 nodes and therefore n + 2 threads. Every thread points at an inorder neighbour, and the header is the neighbour of exactly two nodes.

Step by step.

  1. The leftmost node has no left child, so its left thread points to its inorder predecessor, which is the header.
  2. The rightmost node has no right child, so its right thread points to its inorder successor, which is again the header.
  3. Every other thread points at a real node, so exactly 2 threads reach the header.
  4. Check the count: n + 2 threads in all, of which 2 go to the header and n to real nodes.

Answer: Option (C) — 2

Common trap. Answering 1 by thinking only the rightmost node needs the header, or n by counting one header pointer per node.

Takeaway. The header closes the inorder walk into a cycle, so the traversal can stop on returning to it instead of testing for NULL.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A binary tree has root 10. Its left child is 5 with children 2 and 7. Its right child is 15 with left child 12 and right child 20, and 12 has a left child 11 and no right child. The tree is converted to a fully threaded binary tree. How many nodes have their right pointer replaced by a thread?
questions.question_html: A binary tree has root 10. Its left child is 5 with children 2 and 7. Its right child is 15 with left child 12 and right child 20, and 12 has a left child 11 and no right child. The tree is converted to a fully threaded binary tree. How many nodes have their right pointer replaced by a thread?
questions.solution: Concept. A right pointer becomes a thread exactly for those nodes that have no right child. The left pointers are a separate question.Step by step.List the nodes with no right child: 2 (leaf), 7 (leaf), 12 (only a left child), 11 (leaf) and 20 (leaf).Nodes that do have a right child: 10 (child 15), 5 (child 7) and 15 (child 20). They keep a real right pointer.So 5 nodes carry a right thread.For contrast, nodes with no left child are 2, 7, 11 and 20, that is 4, so counting both kinds of thread would wrongly give 9.Answer: 5Common trap. Answering 4 by counting leaves only: node 12 is not a leaf, but it still has no right child and therefore still carries a right thread.Takeaway. Threads are per missing child pointer, not per leaf.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. A right pointer becomes a thread exactly for those nodes that have no right child. The left pointers are a separate question.

Step by step.

  1. List the nodes with no right child: 2 (leaf), 7 (leaf), 12 (only a left child), 11 (leaf) and 20 (leaf).
  2. Nodes that do have a right child: 10 (child 15), 5 (child 7) and 15 (child 20). They keep a real right pointer.
  3. So 5 nodes carry a right thread.
  4. For contrast, nodes with no left child are 2, 7, 11 and 20, that is 4, so counting both kinds of thread would wrongly give 9.

Answer: 5

Common trap. Answering 4 by counting leaves only: node 12 is not a leaf, but it still has no right child and therefore still carries a right thread.

Takeaway. Threads are per missing child pointer, not per leaf.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: The operators +, −, * have their usual precedence and all are left associative. What is the postfix form of a + b * c − d?
questions.question_html: The operators +, −, * have their usual precedence and all are left associative. What is the postfix form of a + b * c − d?
options: a b + c * d −
a b c * + d −
a b c + * d −
a b c * d + −
questions.solution: Concept. Postfix is the postorder traversal of the expression tree: both operands of an operator appear before the operator itself, and the tree already encodes precedence and associativity.Step by step.* binds tighter than + and −, so the expression parses as (a + (b * c)) − d.Innermost b * c becomes b c *.a + (b c *) becomes a b c * +.(a b c * +) − d becomes a b c * + d −.Answer: Option (B) — a b c * + d −Common trap. Option (A) is (a + b) * c − d, which ignores precedence, and option (C) is a * (b + c) − d.Takeaway. Convert by tree, not by eye: postfix of a node is postfix(left) postfix(right) operator.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Postfix is the postorder traversal of the expression tree: both operands of an operator appear before the operator itself, and the tree already encodes precedence and associativity.

Step by step.

  1. * binds tighter than + and −, so the expression parses as (a + (b * c)) − d.
  2. Innermost b * c becomes b c *.
  3. a + (b c *) becomes a b c * +.
  4. (a b c * +) − d becomes a b c * + d −.

Answer: Option (B) — a b c * + d −

Common trap. Option (A) is (a + b) * c − d, which ignores precedence, and option (C) is a * (b + c) − d.

Takeaway. Convert by tree, not by eye: postfix of a node is postfix(left) postfix(right) operator.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Which traversal of an expression tree produces the prefix form of the expression?
questions.question_html: Which traversal of an expression tree produces the prefix form of the expression?
options: inorder
postorder
preorder
level order
questions.solution: Concept. In an expression tree each internal node is an operator and each leaf an operand, so the three depth-first orders give the three notations.Step by step.Preorder visits the operator before its operands, which is exactly prefix notation.Postorder visits the operator after both operands, which is postfix notation.Inorder visits left, operator, right, which reproduces infix — without the parentheses that the tree itself encodes.Answer: Option (C) — preorderCommon trap. Choosing inorder and expecting the original bracketed string; inorder alone is ambiguous for a + b * c and (a + b) * c.Takeaway. preorder = prefix, postorder = postfix, inorder = infix without brackets.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. In an expression tree each internal node is an operator and each leaf an operand, so the three depth-first orders give the three notations.

Step by step.

  1. Preorder visits the operator before its operands, which is exactly prefix notation.
  2. Postorder visits the operator after both operands, which is postfix notation.
  3. Inorder visits left, operator, right, which reproduces infix — without the parentheses that the tree itself encodes.

Answer: Option (C) — preorder

Common trap. Choosing inorder and expecting the original bracketed string; inorder alone is ambiguous for a + b * c and (a + b) * c.

Takeaway. preorder = prefix, postorder = postfix, inorder = infix without brackets.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Evaluate the postfix expression 5 3 + 8 2 − * 4 /. Every intermediate value is exact and the division is exact. Give the value.
questions.question_html: Evaluate the postfix expression 5 3 + 8 2 − * 4 /. Every intermediate value is exact and the division is exact. Give the value.
questions.solution: Concept. Postfix is evaluated with one stack: push every operand, and on an operator pop the right operand first and then the left.Step by step.Push 5, push 3; on +: pop 3 and 5, push 5 + 3 = 8. Stack: 8.Push 8, push 2; on −: pop 2 and 8, push 8 − 2 = 6. Stack: 8, 6.On *: pop 6 and 8, push 8 × 6 = 48. Stack: 48.Push 4; on /: pop 4 and 48, push 48 / 4 = 12.Answer: 12Common trap. Popping in the wrong order at the subtraction, computing 2 − 8 = −6 and finishing with −12.Takeaway. The first pop is the right operand; for − and / the order changes the answer.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Postfix is evaluated with one stack: push every operand, and on an operator pop the right operand first and then the left.

Step by step.

  1. Push 5, push 3; on +: pop 3 and 5, push 5 + 3 = 8. Stack: 8.
  2. Push 8, push 2; on −: pop 2 and 8, push 8 − 2 = 6. Stack: 8, 6.
  3. On *: pop 6 and 8, push 8 × 6 = 48. Stack: 48.
  4. Push 4; on /: pop 4 and 48, push 48 / 4 = 12.

Answer: 12

Common trap. Popping in the wrong order at the subtraction, computing 2 − 8 = −6 and finishing with −12.

Takeaway. The first pop is the right operand; for − and / the order changes the answer.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Consider an expression tree in which every internal node is a binary operator and every leaf is an operand. Which of the following are TRUE?
questions.question_html: Consider an expression tree in which every internal node is a binary operator and every leaf is an operand. Which of the following are TRUE?
options: Its inorder traversal reproduces the original infix string with all its parentheses.
The number of leaves is one more than the number of internal nodes.
Evaluating the postfix form of the expression needs a stack.
The tree is a full binary tree.
options_html: Its inorder traversal reproduces the original infix string with all its parentheses.
The number of leaves is one more than the number of internal nodes.
Evaluating the postfix form of the expression needs a stack.
The tree is a full binary tree.
questions.solution: Concept. Such a tree is full by construction — every internal node has exactly two children — and the leaf/internal-node identity follows from that.Step by step.(D) true: every internal node is a binary operator with two operands as children.(B) true: in a full binary tree L = I + 1. With 9 operators there are 10 operands, and the token count 2I + 1 agrees.(C) true: postfix evaluation pushes operands and pops on operators, so it needs a stack of depth up to the tree height.(A) false: inorder gives the infix order but no parentheses, so (a + b) * c and a + b * c produce the same inorder string a + b * c.Answer: Options (B), (C), (D)Common trap. Believing the tree "remembers" the parentheses in its inorder; the shape carries them, the inorder string does not.Takeaway. Expression trees are full binary trees, so leaves = operators + 1 and tokens = 2 × operators + 1.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Such a tree is full by construction — every internal node has exactly two children — and the leaf/internal-node identity follows from that.

Step by step.

  1. (D) true: every internal node is a binary operator with two operands as children.
  2. (B) true: in a full binary tree L = I + 1. With 9 operators there are 10 operands, and the token count 2I + 1 agrees.
  3. (C) true: postfix evaluation pushes operands and pops on operators, so it needs a stack of depth up to the tree height.
  4. (A) false: inorder gives the infix order but no parentheses, so (a + b) * c and a + b * c produce the same inorder string a + b * c.

Answer: Options (B), (C), (D)

Common trap. Believing the tree "remembers" the parentheses in its inorder; the shape carries them, the inorder string does not.

Takeaway. Expression trees are full binary trees, so leaves = operators + 1 and tokens = 2 × operators + 1.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: The expression a + b * c − d parses, with the usual precedence and left associativity, as (a + (b * c)) − d. In its expression tree, how many nodes lie in the left subtree of the root?
questions.question_html: The expression a + b * c − d parses, with the usual precedence and left associativity, as (a + (b * c)) − d. In its expression tree, how many nodes lie in the left subtree of the root?
questions.solution: Concept. The root of the expression tree is the last operator applied, and its subtrees are the two operands of that operator.Step by step.The outermost operator is −, so it is the root.Its left operand is the subexpression a + (b * c), whose tree is + with children a and *, and * has children b and c.That is 5 nodes: +, a, *, b, c.Its right operand is the single leaf d, so the whole tree has 7 nodes.Answer: Option (A) — 5Common trap. Answering 3 by counting only the operators and the leaf a, or 4 by forgetting the * node.Takeaway. Count every operator and every operand; a subtree with k operators holds 2k + 1 nodes.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. The root of the expression tree is the last operator applied, and its subtrees are the two operands of that operator.

Step by step.

  1. The outermost operator is −, so it is the root.
  2. Its left operand is the subexpression a + (b * c), whose tree is + with children a and *, and * has children b and c.
  3. That is 5 nodes: +, a, *, b, c.
  4. Its right operand is the single leaf d, so the whole tree has 7 nodes.

Answer: Option (A) — 5

Common trap. Answering 3 by counting only the operators and the leaf a, or 4 by forgetting the * node.

Takeaway. Count every operator and every operand; a subtree with k operators holds 2k + 1 nodes.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: An expression tree has 9 internal nodes, all of them binary operators, and 10 leaves. Which of the following are TRUE?
questions.question_html: An expression tree has 9 internal nodes, all of them binary operators, and 10 leaves. Which of the following are TRUE?
options: Its postfix form has 19 tokens.
Every internal node has exactly two children.
Its prefix form has 18 tokens.
It has exactly one more leaf than internal node.
options_html: Every internal node has exactly two children.
It has exactly one more leaf than internal node.
questions.solution: Concept. Prefix, infix and postfix forms of the same expression tree contain the same tokens, merely in different orders: I operators plus L operands.Step by step.Token count = I + L = 9 + 10 = 19, so (A) is true and (C), which claims 18, is false.Every internal node is a binary operator, so it has two operands as children: (B) is true.L = I + 1 because 10 = 9 + 1, the standard full-tree identity: (D) is true.Equivalently, a full tree with I internal nodes has 2I + 1 nodes in all, here 19, which matches the token count.Answer: Options (A), (B), (D)Common trap. Believing prefix is shorter than postfix because it "starts with the operator"; the token multiset is identical, so both have 2I + 1 tokens.Takeaway. Any expression tree gives 2I + 1 tokens in each of the three notations.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Prefix, infix and postfix forms of the same expression tree contain the same tokens, merely in different orders: I operators plus L operands.

Step by step.

  1. Token count = I + L = 9 + 10 = 19, so (A) is true and (C), which claims 18, is false.
  2. Every internal node is a binary operator, so it has two operands as children: (B) is true.
  3. L = I + 1 because 10 = 9 + 1, the standard full-tree identity: (D) is true.
  4. Equivalently, a full tree with I internal nodes has 2I + 1 nodes in all, here 19, which matches the token count.

Answer: Options (A), (B), (D)

Common trap. Believing prefix is shorter than postfix because it "starts with the operator"; the token multiset is identical, so both have 2I + 1 tokens.

Takeaway. Any expression tree gives 2I + 1 tokens in each of the three notations.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A binary tree has 20 nodes. Exactly 6 of them have two children and exactly 4 have exactly one child. How many leaves does the tree have?
questions.question_html: A binary tree has 20 nodes. Exactly 6 of them have two children and exactly 4 have exactly one child. How many leaves does the tree have?
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Every node of a binary tree has 0, 1 or 2 children, so the three classes partition the nodes: n = n0 + n1 + n2, where n0 counts leaves.Step by step.The two known classes hold 4 + 6 = 10 nodes.So n0 = 20 − 10 = 10.Check: n0 = n2 + 1 = 7 is not required here, because that identity only holds when n1 = 0; the tree does have one-child nodes, and the partition identity already fixes n0.Answer: 10 leavesCommon trap. Reaching for n0 = n2 + 1 and answering 7. That identity is true for every binary tree, but it relates n0 to n2 only; when n1 ≠ 0 you must also use n = n0 + n1 + n2, and here the partition alone is enough.Takeaway. Start every counting question by writing n = n0 + n1 + n2; add n0 = n2 + 1 only as a second equation.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Every node of a binary tree has 0, 1 or 2 children, so the three classes partition the nodes: n = n0 + n1 + n2, where n0 counts leaves.

Step by step.

  1. The two known classes hold 4 + 6 = 10 nodes.
  2. So n0 = 20 − 10 = 10.
  3. Check: n0 = n2 + 1 = 7 is not required here, because that identity only holds when n1 = 0; the tree does have one-child nodes, and the partition identity already fixes n0.

Answer: 10 leaves

Common trap. Reaching for n0 = n2 + 1 and answering 7. That identity is true for every binary tree, but it relates n0 to n2 only; when n1 ≠ 0 you must also use n = n0 + n1 + n2, and here the partition alone is enough.

Takeaway. Start every counting question by writing n = n0 + n1 + n2; add n0 = n2 + 1 only as a second equation.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A binary tree with 30 nodes is stored in records that carry two child pointers, left and right. How many of the 60 pointer fields hold NULL?
questions.question_html: A binary tree with 30 nodes is stored in records that carry two child pointers, left and right. How many of the 60 pointer fields hold NULL?
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. A tree on n nodes has exactly n − 1 edges, and each edge is stored in exactly one child pointer, so exactly n − 1 of the 2n child pointers are non-NULL.Step by step.Non-NULL child pointers = 30 − 1 = 29, one per non-root node.NULL child pointers = 60 − 29 = 31, which is n + 1.Equivalently, each node except the root consumes one pointer, so 2n − (n − 1) = n + 1.Answer: 31 NULL fieldsCommon trap. Answering 30, one NULL per node. The count is per pointer field, not per node, and it is one more than the number of nodes, not one less.Takeaway. Memorise the pair: a binary tree with n nodes has n + 1 NULL pointers and n − 1 edges.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A tree on n nodes has exactly n − 1 edges, and each edge is stored in exactly one child pointer, so exactly n − 1 of the 2n child pointers are non-NULL.

Step by step.

  1. Non-NULL child pointers = 30 − 1 = 29, one per non-root node.
  2. NULL child pointers = 60 − 29 = 31, which is n + 1.
  3. Equivalently, each node except the root consumes one pointer, so 2n − (n − 1) = n + 1.

Answer: 31 NULL fields

Common trap. Answering 30, one NULL per node. The count is per pointer field, not per node, and it is one more than the number of nodes, not one less.

Takeaway. Memorise the pair: a binary tree with n nodes has n + 1 NULL pointers and n − 1 edges.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: In a strictly binary tree every node has either 0 or 2 children. Such a tree has 21 nodes with two children. How many nodes does the tree have in total?
questions.question_html: In a strictly binary tree every node has either 0 or 2 children. Such a tree has 21 nodes with two children. How many nodes does the tree have in total?
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. A strictly binary tree is a full binary tree, so n0 = n2 + 1 and the total is n = 2n2 + 1.Step by step.Leaves: n0 = 21 + 1 = 22.Total: 21 + 22 = 43, that is 2 × 21 + 1 = 43.Sanity check with edges: 43 nodes have 42 edges, and each internal node contributes exactly 2 of them.Answer: 43 nodesCommon trap. Answering 42 from 2 × 21, which forgets that the leaves are counted on top of the internal nodes.Takeaway. For a full binary tree: n = 2n2 + 1 = 2n0 − 1.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A strictly binary tree is a full binary tree, so n0 = n2 + 1 and the total is n = 2n2 + 1.

Step by step.

  1. Leaves: n0 = 21 + 1 = 22.
  2. Total: 21 + 22 = 43, that is 2 × 21 + 1 = 43.
  3. Sanity check with edges: 43 nodes have 42 edges, and each internal node contributes exactly 2 of them.

Answer: 43 nodes

Common trap. Answering 42 from 2 × 21, which forgets that the leaves are counted on top of the internal nodes.

Takeaway. For a full binary tree: n = 2n2 + 1 = 2n0 − 1.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A binary tree has 100 nodes, exactly 30 of which are leaves. How many of its nodes have exactly one child?
questions.question_html: A binary tree has 100 nodes, exactly 30 of which are leaves. How many of its nodes have exactly one child?
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Three equations link the node classes: n = n0 + n1 + n2, n0 = n2 + 1, and the edge count n − 1 = n1 + 2n2.Step by step.From n0 = 30: n2 = 30 − 1 = 29.Then n1 = 100 − 30 − 29 = 41.Check against the edge count: n1 + 2n2 = 41 + 58 = 99 = n − 1. Consistent.Answer: 41 nodes with exactly one childCommon trap. Setting n2 = n0 and getting 40. The correct relation is n2 = n0 − 1, which shifts the answer by one.Takeaway. With n0 and n given, the answer is n − 2n0 + 1; verify it against n − 1 = n1 + 2n2.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Three equations link the node classes: n = n0 + n1 + n2, n0 = n2 + 1, and the edge count n − 1 = n1 + 2n2.

Step by step.

  1. From n0 = 30: n2 = 30 − 1 = 29.
  2. Then n1 = 100 − 30 − 29 = 41.
  3. Check against the edge count: n1 + 2n2 = 41 + 58 = 99 = n − 1. Consistent.

Answer: 41 nodes with exactly one child

Common trap. Setting n2 = n0 and getting 40. The correct relation is n2 = n0 − 1, which shifts the answer by one.

Takeaway. With n0 and n given, the answer is n − 2n0 + 1; verify it against n − 1 = n1 + 2n2.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A complete binary tree has 1000 nodes. The root sits at level 0, and nodes are numbered level by level from left to right. How many nodes lie on the deepest level?
questions.question_html: A complete binary tree has 1000 nodes. The root sits at level 0, and nodes are numbered level by level from left to right. How many nodes lie on the deepest level?
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. A complete binary tree fills levels 0 to h − 1 completely and packs level h from the left, so the first h levels hold 2^h − 1 nodes.Step by step.Find the deepest level: 2^9 − 1 = 511 ≤ 1000 , so h = 9.Levels 0 to 8 hold 511 nodes, all of them full.Deepest level: 1000 − 511 = 489 nodes, out of a possible 512.Answer: 489 nodes on level 9Common trap. Subtracting 512 instead of 511, which double-counts the root and gives 488. The fully filled prefix is 2^h − 1, not 2^h.Takeaway. For a complete tree with n nodes, the last level holds n − (2^h − 1) nodes where h = ⌊log₂ n⌋.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A complete binary tree fills levels 0 to h − 1 completely and packs level h from the left, so the first h levels hold 2^h − 1 nodes.

Step by step.

  1. Find the deepest level: 2^9 − 1 = 511 ≤ 1000 < 1023 = 2^10 − 1, so h = 9.
  2. Levels 0 to 8 hold 511 nodes, all of them full.
  3. Deepest level: 1000 − 511 = 489 nodes, out of a possible 512.

Answer: 489 nodes on level 9

Common trap. Subtracting 512 instead of 511, which double-counts the root and gives 488. The fully filled prefix is 2^h − 1, not 2^h.

Takeaway. For a complete tree with n nodes, the last level holds n − (2^h − 1) nodes where h = ⌊log₂ n⌋.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: For a binary tree with n ≥ 1 nodes and height h measured in edges, which of the following are TRUE?
questions.question_html: For a binary tree with n ≥ 1 nodes and height h measured in edges, which of the following are TRUE?
options: The number of leaves is always exactly one more than the number of nodes with two children.
A complete binary tree with n nodes has height ⌊log₂ n⌋.
Every full binary tree is also a complete binary tree.
Every binary tree with at least two nodes has a node with exactly one child.
options_html: The number of leaves is always exactly one more than the number of nodes with two children.
A complete binary tree with n nodes has height ⌊log₂ n⌋.
Every full binary tree is also a complete binary tree.
Every binary tree with at least two nodes has a node with exactly one child.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Two different structural facts are being tested: the leaf/internal identity, which holds for every binary tree, and the relationship between completeness, fullness and height.Step by step.A is TRUE. Counting edges from both ends gives n − 1 = n1 + 2n2 and n = n0 + n1 + n2, so n0 = n2 + 1 for every binary tree, full or not.B is TRUE. Levels 0 to h − 1 are full, so 2^h − 1 , hence h = ⌊log₂ n⌋. For n = 1000 this gives 9.C is FALSE. A full tree only requires every node to have 0 or 2 children. The tree with root 1, left child 2 and right child 3, where 2 has children 4 and 5 and 3 has none, is full but not complete, because level 2 is not packed from the left.D is FALSE. A perfect tree of 3 or 7 nodes has n1 = 0, so it has no one-child node at all.Answer: Options (A) and (B)Common trap. Treating full and complete as synonyms. Full constrains child counts, complete constrains level filling; neither implies the other.Takeaway. Keep the three families apart: full (0 or 2 children), complete (all levels but the last full, last packed left), perfect (all levels full).
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two different structural facts are being tested: the leaf/internal identity, which holds for every binary tree, and the relationship between completeness, fullness and height.

Step by step.

  1. A is TRUE. Counting edges from both ends gives n − 1 = n1 + 2n2 and n = n0 + n1 + n2, so n0 = n2 + 1 for every binary tree, full or not.
  2. B is TRUE. Levels 0 to h − 1 are full, so 2^h − 1 < n ≤ 2^(h+1) − 1, hence h = ⌊log₂ n⌋. For n = 1000 this gives 9.
  3. C is FALSE. A full tree only requires every node to have 0 or 2 children. The tree with root 1, left child 2 and right child 3, where 2 has children 4 and 5 and 3 has none, is full but not complete, because level 2 is not packed from the left.
  4. D is FALSE. A perfect tree of 3 or 7 nodes has n1 = 0, so it has no one-child node at all.

Answer: Options (A) and (B)

Common trap. Treating full and complete as synonyms. Full constrains child counts, complete constrains level filling; neither implies the other.

Takeaway. Keep the three families apart: full (0 or 2 children), complete (all levels but the last full, last packed left), perfect (all levels full).

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: How many structurally different binary trees have exactly 6 nodes and height exactly 5, where the height is the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf and left and right children are distinguished?
questions.question_html: How many structurally different binary trees have exactly 6 nodes and height exactly 5, where the height is the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf and left and right children are distinguished?
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Height 5 with only 6 nodes forces the shape: the longest root-to-leaf path uses all 5 edges, so every one of the 6 nodes lies on that single path and each node has exactly one child except the last.Step by step.A tree of 6 nodes has height at most 5, and height 5 is reached only by a chain.A chain of 6 nodes has 5 edges, and each edge independently goes to a left child or to a right child.So the count is 2^5 = 32. They are all distinct because the sequence of left/right choices differs.Cross-check: the number of 6-node binary trees of height at most 5 is the Catalan number C_6 = 132, and only the chains are subtracted from it, which is consistent with 32 < 132.Answer: 32 treesCommon trap. Answering 2^6 = 64 by counting one choice per node. The choices are per edge, and a chain of 6 nodes has 5 edges.Takeaway. A chain on n nodes has 2^(n−1) distinct orientations; this is the standard witness that preorder plus postorder does not determine a binary tree.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Height 5 with only 6 nodes forces the shape: the longest root-to-leaf path uses all 5 edges, so every one of the 6 nodes lies on that single path and each node has exactly one child except the last.

Step by step.

  1. A tree of 6 nodes has height at most 5, and height 5 is reached only by a chain.
  2. A chain of 6 nodes has 5 edges, and each edge independently goes to a left child or to a right child.
  3. So the count is 2^5 = 32. They are all distinct because the sequence of left/right choices differs.
  4. Cross-check: the number of 6-node binary trees of height at most 5 is the Catalan number C_6 = 132, and only the chains are subtracted from it, which is consistent with 32 < 132.

Answer: 32 trees

Common trap. Answering 2^6 = 64 by counting one choice per node. The choices are per edge, and a chain of 6 nodes has 5 edges.

Takeaway. A chain on n nodes has 2^(n−1) distinct orientations; this is the standard witness that preorder plus postorder does not determine a binary tree.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A binary tree with distinct keys has inorder A B C D E F and postorder B A D F E C. What is its preorder traversal?
questions.question_html: A binary tree with distinct keys has inorder A B C D E F and postorder B A D F E C. What is its preorder traversal?
options: C A B E D F
C A B E F D
C B A E D F
A B C D E F
options_html: C A B E D F
C A B E F D
C B A E D F
A B C D E F
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Inorder fixes which keys fall left and right of a root; postorder names the root last. Together they rebuild the tree, and the preorder is then read off the rebuilt tree.Step by step.Postorder ends in C, so the root is C. Inorder splits as A B | C | D E F.Left subtree: inorder A B, postorder B A, so the root is A with B as its right child.Right subtree: inorder D E F, postorder D F E, so the root is E with left child D and right child F.Preorder (root, left, right): C, then A B, then E D F → C A B E D F.Answer: C A B E D FCommon trap. Reading postorder left to right and assuming the first symbol is a root. The root is always the last symbol of postorder.Takeaway. Rebuild first, then read the requested traversal; never guess the traversal order from the two given strings.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Inorder fixes which keys fall left and right of a root; postorder names the root last. Together they rebuild the tree, and the preorder is then read off the rebuilt tree.

Step by step.

  1. Postorder ends in C, so the root is C. Inorder splits as A B | C | D E F.
  2. Left subtree: inorder A B, postorder B A, so the root is A with B as its right child.
  3. Right subtree: inorder D E F, postorder D F E, so the root is E with left child D and right child F.
  4. Preorder (root, left, right): C, then A B, then E D F → C A B E D F.

Answer: C A B E D F

Common trap. Reading postorder left to right and assuming the first symbol is a root. The root is always the last symbol of postorder.

Takeaway. Rebuild first, then read the requested traversal; never guess the traversal order from the two given strings.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A binary tree with distinct keys has preorder 1 2 4 8 9 5 3 6 7 and inorder 8 4 9 2 5 1 6 3 7. What is its postorder traversal?
questions.question_html: A binary tree with distinct keys has preorder 1 2 4 8 9 5 3 6 7 and inorder 8 4 9 2 5 1 6 3 7. What is its postorder traversal?
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Preorder names the root first, inorder splits the remaining keys into the left and right subtrees. Rebuilding bottom-up and printing left, right, root gives the postorder.Step by step.Root 1; inorder splits as 8 4 9 2 5 | 1 | 6 3 7.Left subtree, preorder 2 4 8 9 5, inorder 8 4 9 2 5: root 2, left 4(8, 9), right 5.Right subtree, preorder 3 6 7, inorder 6 3 7: root 3, left 6, right 7.Postorder: 8 9 4, 5, 2, then 6, 7, 3, then 1 → 8 9 4 5 2 6 7 3 1.Answer: 8 9 4 5 2 6 7 3 1Common trap. Swapping the left and right children of the root, which yields the option ending ... 2 7 6 3 1. Preorder and inorder both carry the left-right distinction, so the split must be done exactly.Takeaway. The left subtree of the root is exactly the keys before the root in inorder, and their preorder is exactly the matching prefix of preorder.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Preorder names the root first, inorder splits the remaining keys into the left and right subtrees. Rebuilding bottom-up and printing left, right, root gives the postorder.

Step by step.

  1. Root 1; inorder splits as 8 4 9 2 5 | 1 | 6 3 7.
  2. Left subtree, preorder 2 4 8 9 5, inorder 8 4 9 2 5: root 2, left 4(8, 9), right 5.
  3. Right subtree, preorder 3 6 7, inorder 6 3 7: root 3, left 6, right 7.
  4. Postorder: 8 9 4, 5, 2, then 6, 7, 3, then 1 → 8 9 4 5 2 6 7 3 1.

Answer: 8 9 4 5 2 6 7 3 1

Common trap. Swapping the left and right children of the root, which yields the option ending ... 2 7 6 3 1. Preorder and inorder both carry the left-right distinction, so the split must be done exactly.

Takeaway. The left subtree of the root is exactly the keys before the root in inorder, and their preorder is exactly the matching prefix of preorder.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A binary tree with distinct keys has preorder A B C D E F G H and inorder C B D A F E H G. How many leaves does the tree have?
questions.question_html: A binary tree with distinct keys has preorder A B C D E F G H and inorder C B D A F E H G. How many leaves does the tree have?
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Rebuild the tree from the two traversals, then count nodes with no children. A leaf is exactly a node that has neither a left nor a right child.Step by step.Root A; inorder splits as C B D | A | F E H G.Left subtree (preorder B C D, inorder C B D): root B with children C and D. Both are leaves.Right subtree (preorder E F G H, inorder F E H G): root E, left child F, right subtree with preorder G H and inorder H G gives root G with left child H and no right child.Leaves: C, D, F, H → 4 leaves.Check with the identity: internal nodes with two children are A, B, E (and G has one child), so n2 = 3 and n0 = n2 + 1 = 4. Consistent.Answer: 4 leavesCommon trap. Counting only the deepest nodes, which misses F and C; or forgetting that G has a single child, so it is not a leaf.Takeaway. Leaves sit at several depths. Rebuild the shape first and then read off the leaves, or use n0 = n2 + 1 once the two-child nodes are known.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Rebuild the tree from the two traversals, then count nodes with no children. A leaf is exactly a node that has neither a left nor a right child.

Step by step.

  1. Root A; inorder splits as C B D | A | F E H G.
  2. Left subtree (preorder B C D, inorder C B D): root B with children C and D. Both are leaves.
  3. Right subtree (preorder E F G H, inorder F E H G): root E, left child F, right subtree with preorder G H and inorder H G gives root G with left child H and no right child.
  4. Leaves: C, D, F, H → 4 leaves.
  5. Check with the identity: internal nodes with two children are A, B, E (and G has one child), so n2 = 3 and n0 = n2 + 1 = 4. Consistent.

Answer: 4 leaves

Common trap. Counting only the deepest nodes, which misses F and C; or forgetting that G has a single child, so it is not a leaf.

Takeaway. Leaves sit at several depths. Rebuild the shape first and then read off the leaves, or use n0 = n2 + 1 once the two-child nodes are known.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE for binary trees whose keys are all distinct?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements are TRUE for binary trees whose keys are all distinct?
options: If the preorder and the postorder traversals of a full binary tree are both known, the tree is uniquely determined.
The preorder traversal of a binary search tree lists its keys in increasing order.
Two different binary trees can have the same preorder traversal and the same postorder traversal.
The postorder traversal of a binary tree is always the reverse of its preorder traversal.
options_html: If the preorder and the postorder traversals of a full binary tree are both known, the tree is uniquely determined.
The preorder traversal of a binary search tree lists its keys in increasing order.
Two different binary trees can have the same preorder traversal and the same postorder traversal.
The postorder traversal of a binary tree is always the reverse of its preorder traversal.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. A traversal pair determines a tree only when it fixes every left/right decision. The obstruction is a node with exactly one child, which the pair cannot tell apart from its mirror.Step by step.A is TRUE. In a full tree every node has 0 or 2 children, so the size of each subtree is read directly from postorder, and the split is unambiguous at every level.B is FALSE. Preorder visits the root first, so for the BST 2(1, 3) it gives 2 1 3. Only the inorder traversal of a BST is sorted.C is TRUE. Take the chain P → Q → R with all children on the left and the chain with all children on the right. Both give preorder P Q R and postorder R Q P.D is FALSE. For 2(1, 3), preorder is 2 1 3 and postorder is 1 3 2, whose reverse is 2 3 1, not 2 1 3.Answer: Options (A) and (C)Common trap. Assuming that any two traversals always pin a binary tree down. Preorder with inorder, or postorder with inorder, always does; preorder with postorder does not, unless fullness removes the one-child ambiguity.Takeaway. The pair that always works is {preorder or postorder} together with inorder. Level order plus inorder also works when all keys are distinct.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A traversal pair determines a tree only when it fixes every left/right decision. The obstruction is a node with exactly one child, which the pair cannot tell apart from its mirror.

Step by step.

  1. A is TRUE. In a full tree every node has 0 or 2 children, so the size of each subtree is read directly from postorder, and the split is unambiguous at every level.
  2. B is FALSE. Preorder visits the root first, so for the BST 2(1, 3) it gives 2 1 3. Only the inorder traversal of a BST is sorted.
  3. C is TRUE. Take the chain P → Q → R with all children on the left and the chain with all children on the right. Both give preorder P Q R and postorder R Q P.
  4. D is FALSE. For 2(1, 3), preorder is 2 1 3 and postorder is 1 3 2, whose reverse is 2 3 1, not 2 1 3.

Answer: Options (A) and (C)

Common trap. Assuming that any two traversals always pin a binary tree down. Preorder with inorder, or postorder with inorder, always does; preorder with postorder does not, unless fullness removes the one-child ambiguity.

Takeaway. The pair that always works is {preorder or postorder} together with inorder. Level order plus inorder also works when all keys are distinct.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A binary tree with distinct keys has preorder P Q R S and postorder S R Q P. How many different binary trees have exactly these two traversals?
questions.question_html: A binary tree with distinct keys has preorder P Q R S and postorder S R Q P. How many different binary trees have exactly these two traversals?
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Preorder visits a root before its descendants and postorder after them. When the two orders are exact reversals, every node must be an ancestor of the next, so the tree is a chain and only the left/right orientation of each edge is free.Step by step.In preorder the next key after P is Q; in postorder the key before P is Q as well, so Q is the only child of P. The same argument repeats for R and S.So the shape is the chain P → Q → R → S, with 3 edges.Each edge is independently a left edge or a right edge, and the orientation never changes preorder or postorder.Count: 2^3 = 8.Answer: 8 treesCommon trap. Answering 1, on the belief that preorder plus postorder always determine the tree. They determine it only when no node has a single child; here every node except the last has one.Takeaway. Preorder and postorder together determine a tree uniquely if and only if the tree is full; otherwise the free choices are exactly the one-child nodes, giving 2^k trees for k such nodes.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Preorder visits a root before its descendants and postorder after them. When the two orders are exact reversals, every node must be an ancestor of the next, so the tree is a chain and only the left/right orientation of each edge is free.

Step by step.

  1. In preorder the next key after P is Q; in postorder the key before P is Q as well, so Q is the only child of P. The same argument repeats for R and S.
  2. So the shape is the chain P → Q → R → S, with 3 edges.
  3. Each edge is independently a left edge or a right edge, and the orientation never changes preorder or postorder.
  4. Count: 2^3 = 8.

Answer: 8 trees

Common trap. Answering 1, on the belief that preorder plus postorder always determine the tree. They determine it only when no node has a single child; here every node except the last has one.

Takeaway. Preorder and postorder together determine a tree uniquely if and only if the tree is full; otherwise the free choices are exactly the one-child nodes, giving 2^k trees for k such nodes.

questions.question: A binary tree with distinct keys has preorder A B C D E F G and postorder C B E G F D A. Which of the following is its inorder traversal?
questions.question_html: A binary tree with distinct keys has preorder A B C D E F G and postorder C B E G F D A. Which of the following is its inorder traversal?
options: C B A E D F G
B C A E D G F
C B A E D G F
C B A D E G F
options_html: C B A E D F G
B C A E D G F
C B A E D G F
C B A D E G F
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. With only preorder and postorder, the subtree sizes must be read from postorder: the postorder of a subtree is a contiguous block ending at that subtree's root, and its length is the size of the subtree.Step by step.Root A. In preorder the next key is B, the root of the left subtree. In postorder B sits at index 1, so the left subtree has 2 nodes and its postorder is C B → B with left child C.The right subtree is the rest: postorder E G F D, preorder D E F G, so its root is D.Inside it, preorder next is E, at index 0 of the postorder E G F, so E has no children.The remaining right subtree has postorder G F and preorder F G: root F with left child G.Inorder (left, root, right): C B, A, E, D, G F → C B A E D G F.Answer: C B A E D G FCommon trap. Placing G as the right child of F. The split comes from postorder, where G precedes F, which makes it the left child. Guessing from the letters' order in preorder produces option (A).Takeaway. For preorder + postorder, always measure a subtree by the position of its root in the postorder block; never assume balanced children.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With only preorder and postorder, the subtree sizes must be read from postorder: the postorder of a subtree is a contiguous block ending at that subtree's root, and its length is the size of the subtree.

Step by step.

  1. Root A. In preorder the next key is B, the root of the left subtree. In postorder B sits at index 1, so the left subtree has 2 nodes and its postorder is C B → B with left child C.
  2. The right subtree is the rest: postorder E G F D, preorder D E F G, so its root is D.
  3. Inside it, preorder next is E, at index 0 of the postorder E G F, so E has no children.
  4. The remaining right subtree has postorder G F and preorder F G: root F with left child G.
  5. Inorder (left, root, right): C B, A, E, D, G F → C B A E D G F.

Answer: C B A E D G F

Common trap. Placing G as the right child of F. The split comes from postorder, where G precedes F, which makes it the left child. Guessing from the letters' order in preorder produces option (A).

Takeaway. For preorder + postorder, always measure a subtree by the position of its root in the postorder block; never assume balanced children.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: In an inorder-threaded binary tree, the left pointer of a node that has no left child is replaced by a thread. Which node does that thread point to?
questions.question_html: In an inorder-threaded binary tree, the left pointer of a node that has no left child is replaced by a thread. Which node does that thread point to?
options: The node's inorder successor
The node's inorder predecessor
The node's parent
The leftmost leaf of the whole tree
options_html: The leftmost leaf of the whole tree
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Threads store the traversal step that the missing pointer would have wasted. A missing left pointer means the node has nothing to its left, so the traversal reaches it straight after its predecessor.Step by step.In inorder, a node is visited after its entire left subtree. If the left subtree is empty, the visit follows the predecessor immediately.So the left thread points to the inorder predecessor, and symmetrically the right thread of a node with no right child points to its inorder successor.For the leftmost node the predecessor does not exist, which is why a fully threaded tree adds a dummy header node as a sentinel.Answer: Its inorder predecessorCommon trap. Mixing up the two directions and saying the left thread points to the successor. The right thread carries the successor; the left thread carries the predecessor.Takeaway. Left thread = predecessor, right thread = successor, both in inorder. The header node stands in when the predecessor or successor does not exist.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Threads store the traversal step that the missing pointer would have wasted. A missing left pointer means the node has nothing to its left, so the traversal reaches it straight after its predecessor.

Step by step.

  1. In inorder, a node is visited after its entire left subtree. If the left subtree is empty, the visit follows the predecessor immediately.
  2. So the left thread points to the inorder predecessor, and symmetrically the right thread of a node with no right child points to its inorder successor.
  3. For the leftmost node the predecessor does not exist, which is why a fully threaded tree adds a dummy header node as a sentinel.

Answer: Its inorder predecessor

Common trap. Mixing up the two directions and saying the left thread points to the successor. The right thread carries the successor; the left thread carries the predecessor.

Takeaway. Left thread = predecessor, right thread = successor, both in inorder. The header node stands in when the predecessor or successor does not exist.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A fully threaded binary tree is one in which every NULL child pointer has been replaced by a thread. Which of the following are TRUE?
questions.question_html: A fully threaded binary tree is one in which every NULL child pointer has been replaced by a thread. Which of the following are TRUE?
options: Such a tree with n nodes contains exactly n + 1 threads.
A binary tree with 13 nodes has 14 NULL child pointers before threading.
Every thread points to the inorder predecessor or the inorder successor of the node that owns it.
The number of threads in such a tree equals the number of its leaves.
options_html: Such a tree with n nodes contains exactly n + 1 threads.
A binary tree with 13 nodes has 14 NULL child pointers before threading.
Every thread points to the inorder predecessor or the inorder successor of the node that owns it.
The number of threads in such a tree equals the number of its leaves.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Threading reuses exactly the NULL pointers, so the thread count is the NULL-pointer count, n + 1, and each thread stores one inorder neighbour.Step by step.A is TRUE. A binary tree with n nodes has 2n child pointers, of which n − 1 are real, leaving n + 1 NULL pointers and therefore n + 1 threads.B is TRUE. 13 + 1 = 14.C is TRUE. That is the definition of an inorder thread: the field that would have held a missing child now holds the neighbour in the inorder sequence.D is FALSE. Threads are counted per missing child pointer, not per leaf. The perfect tree with 7 nodes has 4 leaves but 8 threads.Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)Common trap. Equating threads with leaves. A leaf contributes two threads only if it is the only node at its position; in general a node with one child contributes one thread, so the total is n + 1 regardless of the leaf count.Takeaway. Threads = NULL pointers = n + 1. Leaves = n2 + 1. These agree only in special shapes.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Threading reuses exactly the NULL pointers, so the thread count is the NULL-pointer count, n + 1, and each thread stores one inorder neighbour.

Step by step.

  1. A is TRUE. A binary tree with n nodes has 2n child pointers, of which n − 1 are real, leaving n + 1 NULL pointers and therefore n + 1 threads.
  2. B is TRUE. 13 + 1 = 14.
  3. C is TRUE. That is the definition of an inorder thread: the field that would have held a missing child now holds the neighbour in the inorder sequence.
  4. D is FALSE. Threads are counted per missing child pointer, not per leaf. The perfect tree with 7 nodes has 4 leaves but 8 threads.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Common trap. Equating threads with leaves. A leaf contributes two threads only if it is the only node at its position; in general a node with one child contributes one thread, so the total is n + 1 regardless of the leaf count.

Takeaway. Threads = NULL pointers = n + 1. Leaves = n2 + 1. These agree only in special shapes.

questions.question: Each node of a threaded binary tree stores two pointer fields, with a one-bit tag beside each of them. Why are the tags necessary?
questions.question_html: Each node of a threaded binary tree stores two pointer fields, with a one-bit tag beside each of them. Why are the tags necessary?
options: A thread and a real child pointer occupy the same field, and nothing else distinguishes them.
A thread may point to a node that has already been freed.
Threading doubles the number of nodes in the tree.
The tags record the depth of each node in the tree.
options_html: A thread and a real child pointer occupy the same field, and nothing else distinguishes them.
A thread may point to a node that has already been freed.
Threading doubles the number of nodes in the tree.
The tags record the depth of each node in the tree.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Threading trades a NULL pointer for a traversal link, so the same field must be able to mean two different things. A one-bit tag resolves which meaning is in force.Step by step.Without a tag, the traversal cannot tell whether a non-NULL pointer leads to a child (descend) or to an ancestor (follow the thread).One bit per pointer is enough: 0 for a real child, 1 for a thread.That is why a threaded node costs two extra bits, and why the memory saving comes from dropping the stack, not from dropping a field.Answer: The first optionCommon trap. Believing threading stores the extra information in a new pointer field. It does not: the field is reused, and only a flag is added.Takeaway. Threading is a tagged union of child and thread. Any implementation must carry the tag or lose the ability to traverse.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Threading trades a NULL pointer for a traversal link, so the same field must be able to mean two different things. A one-bit tag resolves which meaning is in force.

Step by step.

  1. Without a tag, the traversal cannot tell whether a non-NULL pointer leads to a child (descend) or to an ancestor (follow the thread).
  2. One bit per pointer is enough: 0 for a real child, 1 for a thread.
  3. That is why a threaded node costs two extra bits, and why the memory saving comes from dropping the stack, not from dropping a field.

Answer: The first option

Common trap. Believing threading stores the extra information in a new pointer field. It does not: the field is reused, and only a flag is added.

Takeaway. Threading is a tagged union of child and thread. Any implementation must carry the tag or lose the ability to traverse.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about inorder-threaded binary trees are TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about inorder-threaded binary trees are TRUE?
options: The inorder successor of a node that has a right child is found in O(1) time.
Threading needs one extra bit per pointer field to mark a thread.
In a preorder-threaded tree the preorder successor of a leaf is reached in O(1) time.
Threading changes the number of nodes in the tree.
options_html: The inorder successor of a node that has a right child is found in O(1) time.
Threading needs one extra bit per pointer field to mark a thread.
In a preorder-threaded tree the preorder successor of a leaf is reached in O(1) time.
Threading changes the number of nodes in the tree.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. A thread is a stored successor. It helps only where the successor would otherwise require a descent, so the cost of finding a successor depends on whether the node has a right subtree.Step by step.A is FALSE. If the node has a right child, its inorder successor is the leftmost node of that right subtree, reached by descending a spine of length up to h. That is O(h), not O(1).B is TRUE. One bit per pointer field separates a thread from a real child.C is TRUE. For a leaf the preorder successor is stored directly as a thread, so it is a single pointer step.D is FALSE. Threading rewrites NULL pointers and adds tags; the node set is unchanged.Answer: Options (B) and (C)Common trap. Assuming threads make every successor step constant time. Only the case where the needed subtree is missing is constant; a real subtree still has to be entered.Takeaway. Threads remove stack use, not descent. A threaded traversal is O(n) overall but individual successor steps may cost O(h).
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A thread is a stored successor. It helps only where the successor would otherwise require a descent, so the cost of finding a successor depends on whether the node has a right subtree.

Step by step.

  1. A is FALSE. If the node has a right child, its inorder successor is the leftmost node of that right subtree, reached by descending a spine of length up to h. That is O(h), not O(1).
  2. B is TRUE. One bit per pointer field separates a thread from a real child.
  3. C is TRUE. For a leaf the preorder successor is stored directly as a thread, so it is a single pointer step.
  4. D is FALSE. Threading rewrites NULL pointers and adds tags; the node set is unchanged.

Answer: Options (B) and (C)

Common trap. Assuming threads make every successor step constant time. Only the case where the needed subtree is missing is constant; a real subtree still has to be entered.

Takeaway. Threads remove stack use, not descent. A threaded traversal is O(n) overall but individual successor steps may cost O(h).

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A fully inorder-threaded binary tree with n nodes is traversed inorder by following threads and descending left spines, without any stack. What is the total time of this traversal, and why?
questions.question_html: A fully inorder-threaded binary tree with n nodes is traversed inorder by following threads and descending left spines, without any stack. What is the total time of this traversal, and why?
options: Θ(n log n), because every thread step is preceded by a descent.
Θ(n²), because finding a successor may require a descent to a leaf each time.
Θ(h), because the traversal only ever walks the left spine.
Θ(n), because across the whole traversal each edge of the tree is descended at most once.
options_html: Θ(n log n), because every thread step is preceded by a descent.
Θ(n²), because finding a successor may require a descent to a leaf each time.
Θ(h), because the traversal only ever walks the left spine.
Θ(n), because across the whole traversal each edge of the tree is descended at most once.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Individual successor steps can cost O(h), but an amortised argument bounds the whole traversal: the descents only ever move downward along edges that are then never re-descended.Step by step.Each of the n nodes is printed exactly once, which is already Ω(n).Every left-spine descent moves down a tree edge, and once a subtree has been traversed the traversal never descends into it again. A tree has n − 1 edges, so all descents together cost O(n).Thread steps cost O(1) each and there are O(n) of them.Total Θ(n), with O(1) amortised per node and O(1) extra space.Answer: Θ(n)Common trap. Multiplying the worst-case O(h) successor cost by n and concluding O(nh). That over-counts: the expensive descents happen along disjoint parts of the tree, not at every step.Takeaway. Amortised analysis is the point of threading: worst-case O(h) per successor, O(n) in total, O(1) space.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Individual successor steps can cost O(h), but an amortised argument bounds the whole traversal: the descents only ever move downward along edges that are then never re-descended.

Step by step.

  1. Each of the n nodes is printed exactly once, which is already Ω(n).
  2. Every left-spine descent moves down a tree edge, and once a subtree has been traversed the traversal never descends into it again. A tree has n − 1 edges, so all descents together cost O(n).
  3. Thread steps cost O(1) each and there are O(n) of them.
  4. Total Θ(n), with O(1) amortised per node and O(1) extra space.

Answer: Θ(n)

Common trap. Multiplying the worst-case O(h) successor cost by n and concluding O(nh). That over-counts: the expensive descents happen along disjoint parts of the tree, not at every step.

Takeaway. Amortised analysis is the point of threading: worst-case O(h) per successor, O(n) in total, O(1) space.
