questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Which of the following statements about AVL trees are TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about AVL trees are TRUE?
options: The balance factor of every node is −1, 0 or 1.
Every complete binary tree satisfies the AVL balance condition.
A rotation preserves the inorder sequence of the keys in the tree.
An AVL tree with 20 nodes cannot have height 5, where height is measured in edges.
options_html: The balance factor of every node is −1, 0 or 1.
Every complete binary tree satisfies the AVL balance condition.
A rotation preserves the inorder sequence of the keys in the tree.
An AVL tree with 20 nodes cannot have height 5, where height is measured in edges.
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  An AVL tree is a binary search tree plus a height invariant, and the rotations used to restore that invariant are chosen so that the ordering of keys never changes.   Step by step.    (A) The invariant is exactly |height(left) − height(right)| ≤ 1 at every node, so the factor lies in {−1, 0, 1}. True.  (B) In a complete binary tree every level except the last is full, so at any node the two subtree heights differ by at most one. True.  (C) A rotation only rewires parent and child pointers inside a subtree whose keys keep their relative order, so the inorder listing is unchanged. True.  (D) The sparsest AVL tree of height h satisfies N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1 with N(0) = 1, N(1) = 2, giving 4, 7, 12, 20 for h = 2, 3, 4, 5. Exactly 20 nodes is enough for height 5, so such a tree exists. False.    Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C); (D) is FALSE.    Common trap.  Treating the minimum-node sequence 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20 as an exclusive bound and concluding that height 5 needs more than 20 nodes. The value 20 is attainable, not exceeded.   Takeaway.  For any “can an AVL tree of n nodes have height h” question, compare n with N(h): the height is possible exactly when N(h) ≤ n ≤ 2 h+1  − 1.

Detailed solution

Step by step.

  1. (A) The invariant is exactly |height(left) − height(right)| ≤ 1 at every node, so the factor lies in {−1, 0, 1}. True.
  2. (B) In a complete binary tree every level except the last is full, so at any node the two subtree heights differ by at most one. True.
  3. (C) A rotation only rewires parent and child pointers inside a subtree whose keys keep their relative order, so the inorder listing is unchanged. True.
  4. (D) The sparsest AVL tree of height h satisfies N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1 with N(0) = 1, N(1) = 2, giving 4, 7, 12, 20 for h = 2, 3, 4, 5. Exactly 20 nodes is enough for height 5, so such a tree exists. False.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C); (D) is FALSE.

Common trap. Treating the minimum-node sequence 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20 as an exclusive bound and concluding that height 5 needs more than 20 nodes. The value 20 is attainable, not exceeded.

questions.question: The keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 are inserted in that order into an empty AVL tree. Which key is at the root of the final tree?
questions.question_html: The keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 are inserted in that order into an empty AVL tree. Which key is at the root of the final tree?
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  Inserting keys in increasing order into an AVL tree triggers repeated single left rotations, and the tree that results is the complete tree of the same size, not a chain.   Step by step.    Insert 1, 2, 3: 3 creates a right-right chain at 1, so one left rotation makes 2 the root with children 1 and 3.  Insert 4: it becomes the right child of 3. Balance factors stay within ±1.  Insert 5: it makes 3’s right subtree a chain 4–5, so a left rotation at 3 lifts 4 above 3 and 5. The root 2 now has left height 1 and right height 2.  Insert 6: the right subtree becomes 4 with children 3 and 5, and 5 gains the right child 6. The factor at 2 reaches −2, so a left rotation at 2 lifts 4 to the root: 4 with left child 2 (children 1 and 3) and right child 5 (right child 6).  Insert 7: it makes 6’s right subtree a chain, so a left rotation at 5 lifts 6 above 5 and 7.  The root stays 4, and the tree is 4 with left child 2 (children 1, 3) and right child 6 (children 5, 7), the complete tree on seven keys.    Answer: Option (C), 4.    Common trap.  Guessing the middle key 4 because it is the median. That happens to be right here, but the median argument is not the reason and it fails for other sizes; also easy to answer 5 by forgetting the final rotation after inserting 6.   Takeaway.  Sorted insertion into an AVL tree builds a complete tree level by level. For seven keys the complete tree has root 4, and four elementary rotations are performed in total.

Detailed solution

Step by step.

  1. Insert 1, 2, 3: 3 creates a right-right chain at 1, so one left rotation makes 2 the root with children 1 and 3.
  2. Insert 4: it becomes the right child of 3. Balance factors stay within ±1.
  3. Insert 5: it makes 3’s right subtree a chain 4–5, so a left rotation at 3 lifts 4 above 3 and 5. The root 2 now has left height 1 and right height 2.
  4. Insert 6: the right subtree becomes 4 with children 3 and 5, and 5 gains the right child 6. The factor at 2 reaches −2, so a left rotation at 2 lifts 4 to the root: 4 with left child 2 (children 1 and 3) and right child 5 (right child 6).
  5. Insert 7: it makes 6’s right subtree a chain, so a left rotation at 5 lifts 6 above 5 and 7.
  6. The root stays 4, and the tree is 4 with left child 2 (children 1, 3) and right child 6 (children 5, 7), the complete tree on seven keys.

Answer: Option (C), 4.

Common trap. Guessing the middle key 4 because it is the median. That happens to be right here, but the median argument is not the reason and it fails for other sizes; also easy to answer 5 by forgetting the final rotation after inserting 6.

Takeaway. Sorted insertion into an AVL tree builds a complete tree level by level. For seven keys the complete tree has root 4, and four elementary rotations are performed in total.

questions.question: The keys 100, 50, 150, 25, 75, 60, 90, 55, 58 are inserted in that order into an empty AVL tree. Counting a single rotation as one elementary rotation and a double rotation as two, how many elementary rotations does the whole insertion sequence perform?
questions.question_html: The keys 100, 50, 150, 25, 75, 60, 90, 55, 58 are inserted in that order into an empty AVL tree. Counting a single rotation as one elementary rotation and a double rotation as two, how many elementary rotations does the whole insertion sequence perform?
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  A rotation is performed only when some node reaches a balance factor of ±2. A single rotation repairs an outside case (LL or RR), a double rotation repairs an inside case (LR or RL).   Step by step.    100, 50, 150, 25, 75: the tree is 100 with left child 50 (children 25 and 75) and right child 150. All factors are within ±1.  60 becomes the left child of 75, and 90 the right child of 75. At 50 the left height is 1 and the right height is 2, factor −1; no rotation.  55 becomes the left child of 60. At 60 the left height is 1 and the right 0, factor +1; at 50 the left height is 1 and the right height is 3, factor −2.  At node 50 the taller child 75 has factor +1, the opposite direction, so this is an RL case: a right rotation at 75 followed by a left rotation at 50, two elementary rotations. Node 60 now sits above 50 and 75.  58 descends 100 → 50 → 60 → 55 and becomes the right child of 55. At 55 the factor is −1, at 60 the left height is 2 against 0 on the right, factor +2.  At node 60 the taller child 55 has factor −1, the opposite direction, so this is an LR case: a left rotation at 55 then a right rotation at 60, two more elementary rotations. Node 58 sits above 55 and 60.  Total: 2 + 2 = 4 elementary rotations. The final root is 75, with preorder 75, 50, 25, 58, 55, 60, 100, 90, 150.    Answer: 4.    Common trap.  Counting each double rotation as one event and answering 2, or counting the whole insertion as needing a rotation at every ancestor and answering far too many. Also easy to rotate at 100 rather than at the deepest unbalanced node 50 or 60.   Takeaway.  Walk the insertion path bottom-up and stop at the first node with factor ±2. Compare its sign with the sign of its taller child: same sign means one rotation, opposite sign means two.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A rotation is performed only when some node reaches a balance factor of ±2. A single rotation repairs an outside case (LL or RR), a double rotation repairs an inside case (LR or RL).

Step by step.

  1. 100, 50, 150, 25, 75: the tree is 100 with left child 50 (children 25 and 75) and right child 150. All factors are within ±1.
  2. 60 becomes the left child of 75, and 90 the right child of 75. At 50 the left height is 1 and the right height is 2, factor −1; no rotation.
  3. 55 becomes the left child of 60. At 60 the left height is 1 and the right 0, factor +1; at 50 the left height is 1 and the right height is 3, factor −2.
  4. At node 50 the taller child 75 has factor +1, the opposite direction, so this is an RL case: a right rotation at 75 followed by a left rotation at 50, two elementary rotations. Node 60 now sits above 50 and 75.
  5. 58 descends 100 → 50 → 60 → 55 and becomes the right child of 55. At 55 the factor is −1, at 60 the left height is 2 against 0 on the right, factor +2.
  6. At node 60 the taller child 55 has factor −1, the opposite direction, so this is an LR case: a left rotation at 55 then a right rotation at 60, two more elementary rotations. Node 58 sits above 55 and 60.
  7. Total: 2 + 2 = 4 elementary rotations. The final root is 75, with preorder 75, 50, 25, 58, 55, 60, 100, 90, 150.

Answer: 4.

Common trap. Counting each double rotation as one event and answering 2, or counting the whole insertion as needing a rotation at every ancestor and answering far too many. Also easy to rotate at 100 rather than at the deepest unbalanced node 50 or 60.

Takeaway. Walk the insertion path bottom-up and stop at the first node with factor ±2. Compare its sign with the sign of its taller child: same sign means one rotation, opposite sign means two.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: In a B+ tree of order 3, where the order is the maximum number of children an internal node may have, what is the maximum number of keys an internal node can hold?
questions.question_html: In a B+ tree of order 3, where the order is the maximum number of children an internal node may have, what is the maximum number of keys an internal node can hold?
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  An internal node with k children separates them with k − 1 keys, because each key is a boundary between two neighbouring child pointers. The maximum key count is therefore one less than the maximum child count.   Step by step.    Order m = 3 means at most 3 children per node.  Children and keys are paired as pointer, key, pointer, key, pointer, so keys = children − 1.  Maximum keys = 3 − 1 = 2.  Minimum keys for a non-root node is ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 = 2 − 1 = 1, so a legal internal node holds 1 or 2 keys.    Answer: Option (B), 2.    Common trap.  Reading the order as the key capacity and answering 3. The order is always the child capacity, so the key capacity is m − 1.   Takeaway.  Convert the order to a key range once and reuse it: a node of order m holds between ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 and m − 1 keys, the root being allowed as few as one.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An internal node with k children separates them with k − 1 keys, because each key is a boundary between two neighbouring child pointers. The maximum key count is therefore one less than the maximum child count.

Step by step.

  1. Order m = 3 means at most 3 children per node.
  2. Children and keys are paired as pointer, key, pointer, key, pointer, so keys = children − 1.
  3. Maximum keys = 3 − 1 = 2.
  4. Minimum keys for a non-root node is ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 = 2 − 1 = 1, so a legal internal node holds 1 or 2 keys.

Answer: Option (B), 2.

Common trap. Reading the order as the key capacity and answering 3. The order is always the child capacity, so the key capacity is m − 1.

Takeaway. Convert the order to a key range once and reuse it: a node of order m holds between ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 and m − 1 keys, the root being allowed as few as one.

questions.question: A B-tree of order 4 has height 3, measured in edges from the root, and every node other than the root holds at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 keys. What is the minimum number of keys such a tree can contain?
questions.question_html: A B-tree of order 4 has height 3, measured in edges from the root, and every node other than the root holds at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 keys. What is the minimum number of keys such a tree can contain?
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  The minimum key count is obtained by making every node as empty as the rules allow, which minimises both the number of nodes per level and the keys inside each node.   Step by step.    Order m = 4 gives a minimum of ⌈4/2⌉ = 2 children and therefore ⌈4/2⌉ − 1 = 1 key for every non-root node.  The root must have at least 2 children when the tree has more than one node, so it holds 1 key.  Level 1: 2 nodes, 1 key each, 2 keys.  Level 2: each level-1 node has 2 children, so 4 nodes, 1 key each, 4 keys.  Level 3: 8 nodes, 1 key each, 8 keys.  Total = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 keys.    Answer: Option (C), 15.    Common trap.  Using 2 keys per node because the maximum is 3, which gives 45, or forgetting the root’s single key and answering 14.   Takeaway.  Minimum keys at height h in a B-tree of order m is 1 + 2·(⌈m/2⌉) + 2·(⌈m/2⌉) 2  + …, with each term weighted by the minimum keys per node; here every weight is 1, so the sum is just the node count.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Which of the following statements about B-trees are TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about B-trees are TRUE?
options: All leaves of a B-tree lie at the same level.
A B-tree of order m stores at most m − 1 keys in a node.
When a node overflows, its median key moves up into the parent node.
A B-tree may store the same key in more than one node.
options_html: All leaves of a B-tree lie at the same level.
A B-tree of order m stores at most m − 1 keys in a node.
When a node overflows, its median key moves up into the parent node.
A B-tree may store the same key in more than one node.
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  A B-tree is a balanced multiway search tree: every root-to-leaf path has the same length, every node holds a bounded number of sorted keys, and overflow is handled by splitting rather than by growing one branch.   Step by step.    (A) Equal leaf depth is part of the definition, which is what keeps every search the same length. True.  (B) Order m bounds the children at m and the keys at m − 1, since k children need k − 1 separators. True.  (C) A split promotes the median of the overflowing node to the parent and divides the rest into two nodes. True.  (D) A key appears exactly once in a B-tree; duplication of separator keys is a B+ tree property, not a B-tree one. False.    Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C); (D) is FALSE.    Common trap.  Mixing the B-tree and B+ tree definitions. In a B-tree each key is stored once and may carry a record pointer at any node; in a B+ tree keys are repeated, with all records at the leaves.   Takeaway.  Three facts cover most B-tree theory questions: equal leaf depth, keys between ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 and m − 1 per non-root node, and split by promoting the median.

  2. (B) Order m bounds the children at m and the keys at m − 1, since k children need k − 1 separators. True.

  4. (D) A key appears exactly once in a B-tree; duplication of separator keys is a B+ tree property, not a B-tree one. False.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C); (D) is FALSE.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Which of the following statements about B+ trees are TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about B+ trees are TRUE?
options: In a B+ tree, a successful search for a key always ends at a leaf.
A root-to-leaf path in a B+ tree of height h, measured in edges, visits at most h + 1 nodes.
Deleting a key from a B+ tree may leave every internal node unchanged.
A B+ tree stores each key exactly once in the whole tree.
options_html: In a B+ tree, a successful search for a key always ends at a leaf.
A root-to-leaf path in a B+ tree of height h, measured in edges, visits at most h + 1 nodes.
Deleting a key from a B+ tree may leave every internal node unchanged.
A B+ tree stores each key exactly once in the whole tree.
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  In a B+ tree the internal nodes form an index that only routes the search; every record, and therefore every key that carries data, lives in the leaf level, and the leaves are chained in key order.   Step by step.    (A) Internal nodes hold separator keys that merely direct the descent; the matching record is always found in a leaf. True.  (B) A path of h edges passes through h + 1 nodes counting the root and the leaf. True.  (C) If the leaf still has enough keys after the removal and the deleted key is not a separator in an ancestor, no internal node changes at all. True.  (D) A key that acts as a separator in an internal node is stored again in the leaf that holds its record, so keys can appear more than once. False.    Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C); (D) is FALSE.    Common trap.  Assuming a deletion must ripple up to the root. Only an underfull leaf, or the removal of a separator key, forces a change above the leaf level.   Takeaway.  Remember the division of labour: internal nodes route, leaves store and are linked. Point queries cost the height, range queries cost the height plus the leaves scanned.

  4. (D) A key that acts as a separator in an internal node is stored again in the leaf that holds its record, so keys can appear more than once. False.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A B-tree of order 5 holds more than one node and has height 1, that is a root plus one level of leaves. Every node other than the root holds at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 keys. What is the minimum number of keys the tree can contain?
questions.question_html: A B-tree of order 5 holds more than one node and has height 1, that is a root plus one level of leaves. Every node other than the root holds at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 keys. What is the minimum number of keys the tree can contain?
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  The occupancy floor is what makes a B-tree dense: a node may not be arbitrarily empty, so a given height forces a minimum number of keys.   Step by step.    Order m = 5, so every non-root node holds at least ⌈5/2⌉ − 1 = 3 − 1 = 2 keys and has at least 3 children.  A root with more than one node in the tree must have at least 2 children, and 2 children need 1 key.  Height 1 means exactly two levels, so there are two leaves, each holding its minimum of 2 keys.  Total = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 keys.    Answer: Option (B), 5.    Common trap.  Giving each leaf only one key, which would answer 3. A leaf of order 5 must hold at least 2 keys, so one-key leaves are not legal here.   Takeaway.  Always compute the floor ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 first. The floor applies to every non-root node, leaves included, and it is what makes the minimum-height calculation meaningful.

Detailed solution

  2. A root with more than one node in the tree must have at least 2 children, and 2 children need 1 key.
  3. Height 1 means exactly two levels, so there are two leaves, each holding its minimum of 2 keys.
  4. Total = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 keys.

Answer: Option (B), 5.

Common trap. Giving each leaf only one key, which would answer 3. A leaf of order 5 must hold at least 2 keys, so one-key leaves are not legal here.

Takeaway. Always compute the floor ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 first. The floor applies to every non-root node, leaves included, and it is what makes the minimum-height calculation meaningful.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: The keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 are inserted in that order into an empty B-tree of order 3, that is at most 3 children and at most 2 keys per node. Which keys are stored in the root of the final tree?
questions.question_html: The keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 are inserted in that order into an empty B-tree of order 3, that is at most 3 children and at most 2 keys per node. Which keys are stored in the root of the final tree?
options: 30 only
20 only
30 and 40
20 and 40
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  A node that would exceed m − 1 keys splits: its median key rises into the parent and the remaining keys form two nodes. When the root splits, the tree grows one level.   Step by step.    Insert 10 and 20: the root holds [10, 20], which is the maximum for order 3.  Insert 30: the root would hold three keys, so it splits. The median 20 goes up into a new root, and [10] and [30] become its two children.  Insert 40: it descends past 20 to the right leaf, which becomes [30, 40].  Insert 50: that leaf would hold [30, 40, 50], so it splits. Its median 40 rises to the root, which becomes [20, 40], and the leaf becomes [30] and [50].  Final tree: root [20, 40] with the three leaves [10], [30] and [50].    Answer: Option (D), 20 and 40.    Common trap.  Promoting the largest key 50 instead of the median, or stopping after the first split and reporting 20 alone.   Takeaway.  Splitting always promotes the median, never the maximum or the minimum, and a split can cascade upwards one level at a time.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A node that would exceed m − 1 keys splits: its median key rises into the parent and the remaining keys form two nodes. When the root splits, the tree grows one level.

Step by step.

  1. Insert 10 and 20: the root holds [10, 20], which is the maximum for order 3.
  2. Insert 30: the root would hold three keys, so it splits. The median 20 goes up into a new root, and [10] and [30] become its two children.
  3. Insert 40: it descends past 20 to the right leaf, which becomes [30, 40].
  4. Insert 50: that leaf would hold [30, 40, 50], so it splits. Its median 40 rises to the root, which becomes [20, 40], and the leaf becomes [30] and [50].
  5. Final tree: root [20, 40] with the three leaves [10], [30] and [50].

Answer: Option (D), 20 and 40.

Common trap. Promoting the largest key 50 instead of the median, or stopping after the first split and reporting 20 alone.

Takeaway. Splitting always promotes the median, never the maximum or the minimum, and a split can cascade upwards one level at a time.

questions.question: The single string banana is stored in a standard trie with one node per distinct prefix character and one root node. Counting the root, how many nodes does the trie have?
questions.question_html: The single string banana is stored in a standard trie with one node per distinct prefix character and one root node. Counting the root, how many nodes does the trie have?
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  A standard trie stores one node per distinct prefix of the stored keys, plus a root that represents the empty prefix. A single key of length L therefore contributes exactly L nodes.   Step by step.    Prefixes of banana: the empty prefix, b, ba, ban, bana, banan, banana.  That is 6 non-empty prefixes, so 6 nodes below the root.  Adding the root gives 6 + 1 = 7 nodes.    Answer: Option (D), 7.    Common trap.  Counting the repeated letters as one node because the alphabet is small, which gives 4 or 5, or forgetting the root and answering 6.   Takeaway.  Nodes correspond to prefixes, not to distinct characters. Repetition inside one key still costs one node per position.

  2. That is 6 non-empty prefixes, so 6 nodes below the root.
  3. Adding the root gives 6 + 1 = 7 nodes.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A standard trie is implemented with one array of 26 child pointers per node, each pointer taking 4 bytes, plus a 1-byte end-of-key flag. How many bytes does a single trie node occupy?
questions.question_html: A standard trie is implemented with one array of 26 child pointers per node, each pointer taking 4 bytes, plus a 1-byte end-of-key flag. How many bytes does a single trie node occupy?
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  The array-of-children representation trades memory for O(1) child lookup: every node reserves a slot for every letter of the alphabet whether or not that letter occurs.   Step by step.    Children: 26 slots × 4 bytes = 104 bytes.  End-of-key flag: 1 byte.  Total per node: 104 + 1 = 105 bytes.  Compare this with the n·L + 1 node bound: a trie holding 500 keys of length 8 can reach 4001 nodes, which at 105 bytes each is about 420 KB, most of it empty child slots.    Answer: Option (B), 105 bytes.    Common trap.  Answering 104 by forgetting the end-of-key flag, which is what lets a key end at an internal node; or assuming each node stores only the characters actually present, which is the compressed, not the array-based, representation.   Takeaway.  The array representation makes lookups O(1) per character at the cost of Θ(σ) space per node. Terminating a key needs an explicit flag because keys can end at internal nodes.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: The seven strings ant, ante, anti, bat, batch, ban and band are stored in a standard trie with one node per distinct prefix character and one root node. Counting the root, how many nodes does the trie have?
questions.question_html: The seven strings ant, ante, anti, bat, batch, ban and band are stored in a standard trie with one node per distinct prefix character and one root node. Counting the root, how many nodes does the trie have?
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  The node count equals the number of distinct prefixes of the stored keys, counting the empty prefix as the root. Shared prefixes are counted once, which is exactly where the saving over 7 × 5 comes from.   Step by step.    Under the root, the first characters are a and b, so two nodes at level 1.  Branch a: a → n → t gives ant. From that t the children e and i give ante and anti. So a contributes a, n, t, e, i = 5 nodes.  Branch b: b → a. From that a, one child t and one child n. The t branch adds c and h for batch, so b, a, t, c, h = 5 nodes; the n branch adds d for band, so n and d = 2 more.  Total below the root: 5 + 5 + 2 = 12 nodes.  Adding the root: 13 nodes.    Answer: Option (C), 13.    Common trap.  Counting 7 × 4 characters and forgetting that ant, ante and anti share a, n, t; or forgetting that ban is a proper prefix of band, which is why the node for ban must be marked as an end of key rather than being a leaf.   Takeaway.  Build the trie character by character and count nodes as you create them. A key that is a proper prefix of another ends at an internal node, which needs an explicit end marker.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Which of the following statements about standard tries are TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about standard tries are TRUE?
options: Inserting a key of length L takes O(L) time when each child lookup is O(1).
A trie holding n keys of length at most L has at most n·L + 1 nodes, counting the root.
Two keys that differ in their first character share no node below the root.
In a standard trie, keys are stored only at leaves and never at internal nodes.
options_html: Inserting a key of length L takes O(L) time when each child lookup is O(1).
A trie holding n keys of length at most L has at most n·L + 1 nodes, counting the root.
Two keys that differ in their first character share no node below the root.
In a standard trie, keys are stored only at leaves and never at internal nodes.
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  A trie moves the work from key comparisons to character steps: the path spelling a key is the key, so cost is measured per character and sharing happens along common prefixes.   Step by step.    (A) The insertion follows one child pointer per character and creates a node only where the path is missing, so it costs O(L). True.  (B) Each of the n keys creates at most L new nodes, and the root is one more, so n·L + 1 is a valid upper bound. True.  (C) The root’s children are indexed by first character, so keys with different first characters leave through different children and never meet again. True.  (D) A key that is a proper prefix of another ends at an internal node, which is marked as an end of key; keys are therefore not confined to leaves. False.    Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C); (D) is FALSE.    Common trap.  Carrying over the B+ tree rule that all records live at the leaves. A trie has no such rule, which is why it needs an end-of-key flag.   Takeaway.  Trie cost is O(L) per operation, independent of n, and its size is bounded by the total number of characters stored plus the root.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Which structure answers a prefix query, listing every stored key that begins with a given string, in time proportional to the length of the prefix plus the number of keys reported, in the worst case?
questions.question_html: Which structure answers a prefix query, listing every stored key that begins with a given string, in time proportional to the length of the prefix plus the number of keys reported, in the worst case?
options: A hash table with chaining
A balanced binary search tree
A trie
A sorted array with binary search
options_html: A sorted array with binary search
questions.solution: Detailed solution   Concept.  A prefix query needs the structure to group keys by their leading characters. Only a structure that is organised along characters can walk to the prefix once and then enumerate the subtree beneath it.   Step by step.    A hash table scatters keys by their full value, so keys sharing a prefix land in unrelated buckets and every key must be examined. It gives no bound of the required form.  A balanced binary search tree can find one key starting with the prefix in O(log n) and then scan successors, but the cost includes the log n descent for the first key and it stores characters only implicitly through key comparisons.  A trie walks the prefix in O(L) steps and then traverses the subtree whose nodes are exactly the matching keys, so the cost is O(L + number of keys reported).  A sorted array needs a binary search plus a contiguous scan, and insertion into it is expensive, so it is not the intended answer for the query cost alone.    Answer: Option (C), a trie.    Common trap.  Choosing the hash table because lookups are O(1). That bound is for an exact key match and collapses for prefix queries, which need ordering by character.   Takeaway.  Match the structure to the query: exact match favours hashing, ordered and range queries favour balanced trees, and prefix queries favour tries.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A prefix query needs the structure to group keys by their leading characters. Only a structure that is organised along characters can walk to the prefix once and then enumerate the subtree beneath it.

Step by step.

  1. A hash table scatters keys by their full value, so keys sharing a prefix land in unrelated buckets and every key must be examined. It gives no bound of the required form.
  2. A balanced binary search tree can find one key starting with the prefix in O(log n) and then scan successors, but the cost includes the log n descent for the first key and it stores characters only implicitly through key comparisons.
  3. A trie walks the prefix in O(L) steps and then traverses the subtree whose nodes are exactly the matching keys, so the cost is O(L + number of keys reported).
  4. A sorted array needs a binary search plus a contiguous scan, and insertion into it is expensive, so it is not the intended answer for the query cost alone.

Answer: Option (C), a trie.

Common trap. Choosing the hash table because lookups are O(1). That bound is for an exact key match and collapses for prefix queries, which need ordering by character.

Takeaway. Match the structure to the query: exact match favours hashing, ordered and range queries favour balanced trees, and prefix queries favour tries.

questions.question: A max-heap of n distinct keys is stored in an array A[1..n] with 1-based indexing, the children of A[i] being A[2i] and A[2i+1]. Which one of the following is guaranteed for every valid index?
questions.question_html: A max-heap of n distinct keys is stored in an array A[1..n] with 1-based indexing, the children of A[i] being A[2i] and A[2i+1]. Which one of the following is guaranteed for every valid index?
options: A[i] ≥ A[j] for every pair of indices with i < j
The array is sorted in non-increasing order, so A[i] ≥ A[i+1] for every 1 ≤ i < n
A[i] ≥ A[2i] and A[i] ≥ A[2i+1] whenever those children exist
A[i] ≥ A[i+1] for every 1 ≤ i < n
options_html: A[i] ≥ A[j] for every pair of indices with i < j
The array is sorted in non-increasing order, so A[i] ≥ A[i+1] for every 1 ≤ i < n
A[i] ≥ A[2i] and A[i] ≥ A[2i+1] whenever those children exist
A[i] ≥ A[i+1] for every 1 ≤ i < n
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. A max-heap is a complete binary tree in which every parent is at least as large as each of its children. Written in level order that is exactly the local constraint A[i] ≥ A[2i] and A[i] ≥ A[2i+1] .  Step by step.  The heap property is local: it relates a node only to its two children. It says nothing about siblings. For A = [9, 7, 8, 5, 6, 4, 3] the property holds, yet A[2] = 7 < A[3] = 8 . It also says nothing about the array as a whole, so the array need not be sorted: in that same example A[2] = 7 < A[3] = 8 while the maximum 9 sits at A[1] . Only the parent–child inequality survives for every index.  Answer: Option (C) — a node is at least as large as each of its children.  Why the other options are wrong.  (A) The example above breaks it: 2 < 3 but A[2] = 7 < A[3] = 8 . (B) That is the sorted-array property, which is far stronger than heap order. (D) The same example breaks it as well, since A[2] < A[3] .  Common misconception. Treating a heap as a sorted array. A heap is only partially ordered, and that is precisely what makes it cheap to maintain.  Takeaway. A heap guarantees parent ≥ child and nothing else; the root is the maximum, the rest of the array is arbitrary.

Step by step.

  1. The heap property is local: it relates a node only to its two children.
  2. It says nothing about siblings. For A = [9, 7, 8, 5, 6, 4, 3] the property holds, yet A[2] = 7 < A[3] = 8.
  3. It also says nothing about the array as a whole, so the array need not be sorted: in that same example A[2] = 7 < A[3] = 8 while the maximum 9 sits at A[1].
  4. Only the parent–child inequality survives for every index.

Answer: Option (C) — a node is at least as large as each of its children.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) The example above breaks it: 2 < 3 but A[2] = 7 < A[3] = 8.
  • (B) That is the sorted-array property, which is far stronger than heap order.
  • (D) The same example breaks it as well, since A[2] < A[3].

questions.question: A max-heap of 100 distinct keys is stored in A[1..100]. Which statement about the position of the smallest key is correct?
questions.question_html: A max-heap of 100 distinct keys is stored in A[1..100]. Which statement about the position of the smallest key is correct?
options: It is always stored at A[100].
It is stored at some index in the range 51–100, and each index in that range is possible.
It must be stored at A[2] or A[3].
It may be stored at any index from 1 to 100.
options_html: It is always stored at A[100].
It is stored at some index in the range 51–100, and each index in that range is possible.
It must be stored at A[2] or A[3].
It may be stored at any index from 1 to 100.
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. In a 1-indexed array of n nodes, node i is a leaf exactly when 2i > n , that is when i > ⌊n/2⌋ . Nodes 1..⌊n/2⌋ are internal.  Step by step.  For n = 100, ⌊100/2⌋ = 50 , so nodes 51–100 are exactly the leaves. An internal node has at least one child, and the heap property forces that child to be no larger than the parent. An internal node therefore always has a key smaller than itself somewhere below it, so it can never be the global minimum. The minimum must therefore be a leaf, that is at some index in 51–100. Every leaf position is attainable: place the smallest key at the leaf you want and fill the rest so that each parent dominates its subtree.  Answer: Option (B) — the smallest key is a leaf, at some index in 51–100.  Why the other options are wrong.  (A) A[100] is a leaf, but the minimum may sit at any of the 50 leaves. (C) A[2] and A[3] are internal for n = 100, so neither can hold the minimum; they are where the second largest key may sit. (D) No internal node can hold the minimum.  Common misconception. Mirroring the maximum and expecting the minimum at a fixed cell. The maximum is pinned to the root by the heap property; the minimum is only known to be somewhere on the bottom level.  Takeaway. In a max-heap the maximum is A[1] and the minimum lies among the leaves ⌊n/2⌋+1 to n.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In a 1-indexed array of n nodes, node i is a leaf exactly when 2i > n, that is when i > ⌊n/2⌋. Nodes 1..⌊n/2⌋ are internal.

Step by step.

  1. For n = 100, ⌊100/2⌋ = 50, so nodes 51–100 are exactly the leaves.
  2. An internal node has at least one child, and the heap property forces that child to be no larger than the parent. An internal node therefore always has a key smaller than itself somewhere below it, so it can never be the global minimum.
  3. The minimum must therefore be a leaf, that is at some index in 51–100.
  4. Every leaf position is attainable: place the smallest key at the leaf you want and fill the rest so that each parent dominates its subtree.

Answer: Option (B) — the smallest key is a leaf, at some index in 51–100.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) A[100] is a leaf, but the minimum may sit at any of the 50 leaves.
  • (C) A[2] and A[3] are internal for n = 100, so neither can hold the minimum; they are where the second largest key may sit.
  • (D) No internal node can hold the minimum.

Common misconception. Mirroring the maximum and expecting the minimum at a fixed cell. The maximum is pinned to the root by the heap property; the minimum is only known to be somewhere on the bottom level.

Takeaway. In a max-heap the maximum is A[1] and the minimum lies among the leaves ⌊n/2⌋+1 to n.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Which one of the following arrays of seven distinct keys, read as A[1..7], is a valid max-heap?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following arrays of seven distinct keys, read as A[1..7], is a valid max-heap?
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. For A[1..7] the internal nodes are 1, 2 and 3, with children (2,3), (4,5), (6,7) . Three inequalities decide everything: A[1] ≥ A[2], A[3] ; A[2] ≥ A[4], A[5] ; A[3] ≥ A[6], A[7] .  Step by step.  Check 9, 8, 7, 6, 9, 4, 3 : A[2] = 8 but its child A[5] = 9 , so the parent is smaller than a child. Invalid. Check 8, 9, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3 : the root 8 is smaller than A[2] = 9 . Invalid. Check 9, 6, 8, 7, 5, 4, 3 : A[2] = 6 but its child A[4] = 7 . Invalid. Check 9, 7, 8, 5, 6, 4, 3 : 9 ≥ 7 and 9 ≥ 8; 7 ≥ 5 and 7 ≥ 6; 8 ≥ 4 and 8 ≥ 3. All six inequalities hold, so this is a max-heap.  Answer: Option (D) — 9, 7, 8, 5, 6, 4, 3 is the only valid max-heap.  Why the other options are wrong.  (A) has a child larger than its parent: 9 sits below 8. (B) has a root smaller than its left child. (C) has 7 below 6 at index 4 below index 2.  Common misconception. Scanning the array from left to right and checking only consecutive pairs. Heap order is between a node and the nodes at double and double-plus-one, never between neighbours.  Takeaway. Test A[i] ≥ A[2i] and A[i] ≥ A[2i+1] for the internal nodes only; that is the whole definition.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. For A[1..7] the internal nodes are 1, 2 and 3, with children (2,3), (4,5), (6,7). Three inequalities decide everything: A[1] ≥ A[2], A[3]; A[2] ≥ A[4], A[5]; A[3] ≥ A[6], A[7].

Step by step.

  1. Check 9, 8, 7, 6, 9, 4, 3: A[2] = 8 but its child A[5] = 9, so the parent is smaller than a child. Invalid.
  2. Check 8, 9, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3: the root 8 is smaller than A[2] = 9. Invalid.
  3. Check 9, 6, 8, 7, 5, 4, 3: A[2] = 6 but its child A[4] = 7. Invalid.
  4. Check 9, 7, 8, 5, 6, 4, 3: 9 ≥ 7 and 9 ≥ 8; 7 ≥ 5 and 7 ≥ 6; 8 ≥ 4 and 8 ≥ 3. All six inequalities hold, so this is a max-heap.

Answer: Option (D) — 9, 7, 8, 5, 6, 4, 3 is the only valid max-heap.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) has a child larger than its parent: 9 sits below 8.
  • (B) has a root smaller than its left child.
  • (C) has 7 below 6 at index 4 below index 2.

Common misconception. Scanning the array from left to right and checking only consecutive pairs. Heap order is between a node and the nodes at double and double-plus-one, never between neighbours.

Takeaway. Test A[i] ≥ A[2i] and A[i] ≥ A[2i+1] for the internal nodes only; that is the whole definition.

questions.question:
A min-heap stores n = 1000 keys in A[1..1000]. How many of its nodes have exactly one child?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
A min-heap stores n = 1000 keys in A[1..1000]. How many of its nodes have exactly one child?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. Node i has exactly one child when 2i ≤ n but 2i + 1 > n , that is when 2i = n exactly.  Step by step.  Node i has two children when 2i + 1 ≤ n , one child when 2i = n , and none when 2i > n . So a node with exactly one child exists only when n is even, and then only the single index i = n/2 qualifies. Here n = 1000 is even, so i = 500 has the left child A[1000] and no right child. Every other internal node (1 to 499) has two children, and nodes 501 to 1000 are leaves.  Answer: 1 node — the node at index 500.  Common misconception. Assuming a complete tree must have either 0 or 2 children everywhere. Only the last internal node can be short of a right child, and only when n is even.  Takeaway. In an n-node heap exactly one node has one child when n is even (index n/2), and none when n is odd.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Node i has exactly one child when 2i ≤ n but 2i + 1 > n, that is when 2i = n exactly.

Step by step.

  1. Node i has two children when 2i + 1 ≤ n, one child when 2i = n, and none when 2i > n.
  2. So a node with exactly one child exists only when n is even, and then only the single index i = n/2 qualifies.
  3. Here n = 1000 is even, so i = 500 has the left child A[1000] and no right child.
  4. Every other internal node (1 to 499) has two children, and nodes 501 to 1000 are leaves.

Answer: 1 node — the node at index 500.

Common misconception. Assuming a complete tree must have either 0 or 2 children everywhere. Only the last internal node can be short of a right child, and only when n is even.

Takeaway. In an n-node heap exactly one node has one child when n is even (index n/2), and none when n is odd.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Let H be a binary min-heap holding n ≥ 2 distinct keys in A[1..n]. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Let H be a binary min-heap holding n ≥ 2 distinct keys in A[1..n]. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The second smallest key is stored at A[2] or A[3].
Deleting the minimum and restoring the heap property takes O(log n) time.
Deciding whether an arbitrary key k occurs in H takes O(log n) time in the worst case.
Along every path from the root to a leaf the keys are non-decreasing.
options_html: The second smallest key is stored at A[2] or A[3].
Deleting the minimum and restoring the heap property takes O(log n) time.
Deciding whether an arbitrary key k occurs in H takes O(log n) time in the worst case.
Along every path from the root to a leaf the keys are non-decreasing.
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. Everything below the root is at least as large as the root, and the heap property applies along every parent–child edge, so it holds along every root-to-leaf path. There is no ordering between siblings, which is what limits search.  Step by step.  (A) Every key other than the root is in one of the two subtrees of the root, so the smallest of the remaining keys is the smaller of A[2] and A[3] . True. (B) DELETE-MIN moves the last key to the root, shrinks the heap and sifts down one root-to-leaf path, which has length at most the height ⌊log₂ n⌋. True. (C) A heap offers no way to choose a subtree: both children may contain k or neither, so in the worst case every node is examined, which is Θ(n). False. (D) Each edge satisfies parent ≤ child, so the keys along any root-to-leaf path are non-decreasing. True.  Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are correct.  Why option (C) is not selected.  The heap order does not constrain the relative order of the two subtrees of a node, so a search for k cannot prune either side. Searching a heap is Θ(n) in the worst case, which is why a heap is not a search structure.  Common misconception. Confusing “logarithmic depth” with “logarithmic search”. A binary search tree prunes one subtree; a heap cannot.  Takeaway. A heap gives O(1) access to the extremum, O(log n) insertion and deletion, and Θ(n) arbitrary search.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Everything below the root is at least as large as the root, and the heap property applies along every parent–child edge, so it holds along every root-to-leaf path. There is no ordering between siblings, which is what limits search.

Step by step.

  1. (A) Every key other than the root is in one of the two subtrees of the root, so the smallest of the remaining keys is the smaller of A[2] and A[3]. True.
  2. (B) DELETE-MIN moves the last key to the root, shrinks the heap and sifts down one root-to-leaf path, which has length at most the height ⌊log₂ n⌋. True.
  3. (C) A heap offers no way to choose a subtree: both children may contain k or neither, so in the worst case every node is examined, which is Θ(n). False.
  4. (D) Each edge satisfies parent ≤ child, so the keys along any root-to-leaf path are non-decreasing. True.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are correct.

Why option (C) is not selected.

  • The heap order does not constrain the relative order of the two subtrees of a node, so a search for k cannot prune either side. Searching a heap is Θ(n) in the worst case, which is why a heap is not a search structure.

Common misconception. Confusing “logarithmic depth” with “logarithmic search”. A binary search tree prunes one subtree; a heap cannot.

Takeaway. A heap gives O(1) access to the extremum, O(log n) insertion and deletion, and Θ(n) arbitrary search.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A min-max heap alternates min levels and max levels, the root being on level 0, a min level. Which one of the following is its defining invariant?
questions.question_html: A min-max heap alternates min levels and max levels, the root being on level 0, a min level. Which one of the following is its defining invariant?
options: Every node on a min level is ≤ every key in its own subtree, and every node on a max level is ≥ every key in its own subtree.
Every node on a min level is ≤ its two children only, and every node on a max level is ≥ its two children only.
The keys obey the ordinary heap order along every root-to-leaf path, exactly as in a binary min-heap.
Insertion compares a new key only with its parent, exactly as in an ordinary binary heap.
options_html: Every node on a min level is ≤ every key in its own subtree, and every node on a max level is ≥ every key in its own subtree.
Every node on a min level is ≤ its two children only, and every node on a max level is ≥ its two children only.
The keys obey the ordinary heap order along every root-to-leaf path, exactly as in a binary min-heap.
Insertion compares a new key only with its parent, exactly as in an ordinary binary heap.
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. A min-max heap keeps two orders at once. On a min level the node is the smallest key of its subtree; on a max level it is the largest key of its subtree. The guarantee is against the whole subtree, not merely against the immediate children.  Step by step.  Levels alternate: level 0 min, level 1 max, level 2 min, and so on. The min-level guarantee is what makes the root the global minimum, and the max-level guarantee is what makes the maximum one of the two children of the root. Verifying against the grandchildren is enough in practice, because a child of a min-level node is on a max level and is already ≥ its own children. That is why insertion and deletion compare a new key with its parent and its grandparent, and the cost stays O(log n).  Answer: Option (A) — a min-level node dominates its whole subtree from below, a max-level node from above.  Why the other options are wrong.  (B) Weakening the invariant to the two children only would allow a grandchild smaller than a min-level node, and the root would no longer be the minimum. (C) That is the ordinary binary min-heap, which cannot give O(1) access to the maximum. (D) A min-max heap must compare with the grandparent as well as the parent, which is exactly what the two-level order requires.  Common misconception. Assuming a min-max heap is just a min-heap that also happens to know the maximum. The subtree guarantee is the whole point: it bounds the maximum without a full scan.  Takeaway. Min-max heaps give O(1) access to both the minimum and the maximum and O(log n) insert, delete-min and delete-max.

  1. Levels alternate: level 0 min, level 1 max, level 2 min, and so on.
  2. The min-level guarantee is what makes the root the global minimum, and the max-level guarantee is what makes the maximum one of the two children of the root.
  3. Verifying against the grandchildren is enough in practice, because a child of a min-level node is on a max level and is already ≥ its own children.
  4. That is why insertion and deletion compare a new key with its parent and its grandparent, and the cost stays O(log n).

Answer: Option (A) — a min-level node dominates its whole subtree from below, a max-level node from above.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Weakening the invariant to the two children only would allow a grandchild smaller than a min-level node, and the root would no longer be the minimum.
  • (C) That is the ordinary binary min-heap, which cannot give O(1) access to the maximum.
  • (D) A min-max heap must compare with the grandparent as well as the parent, which is exactly what the two-level order requires.

Common misconception. Assuming a min-max heap is just a min-heap that also happens to know the maximum. The subtree guarantee is the whole point: it bounds the maximum without a full scan.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: BUILD-MAX-HEAP is the bottom-up procedure that calls MAX-HEAPIFY on i = ⌊n/2⌋, ⌊n/2⌋ − 1, …, 1 for an array of n keys. Its tight running time on an arbitrary array is:
questions.question_html: BUILD-MAX-HEAP is the bottom-up procedure that calls MAX-HEAPIFY on i = ⌊n/2⌋, ⌊n/2⌋ − 1, …, 1 for an array of n keys. Its tight running time on an arbitrary array is:
options: Θ(n log n)
Θ(log n)
Θ(n²)
Θ(n)
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. Bottom-up heap construction is linear, not n log n. Most nodes sit near the bottom of the tree and therefore sift down only a short distance.  Step by step.  A node of height h can descend at most h levels, so its MAX-HEAPIFY costs O(h). There are at most ⌈n/2^(h+1)⌉ nodes of height h. Total work is Σₕ ⌈n/2^(h+1)⌉·O(h) = O(n·Σₕ h/2^h) , and Σₕ h/2^h = 2 , a constant. So the total is O(n), and since every key must be read at least once it is Θ(n).  Answer: Option (D) — Θ(n).  Why the other options are wrong.  (A) Θ(n log n) is the cost of inserting the keys one at a time, not of the bottom-up build. (B) Θ(log n) is the cost of a single MAX-HEAPIFY call. (C) No comparison-based heap build is quadratic.  Common misconception. Multiplying “about n/2 calls” by “O(log n) per call” and concluding n log n. The calls are not all deep: the deepest are the fewest.  Takeaway. Bottom-up build-heap is Θ(n); repeated insertion is Θ(n log n) in the worst case.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Bottom-up heap construction is linear, not n log n. Most nodes sit near the bottom of the tree and therefore sift down only a short distance.

Step by step.

  1. A node of height h can descend at most h levels, so its MAX-HEAPIFY costs O(h).
  2. There are at most ⌈n/2^(h+1)⌉ nodes of height h.
  3. Total work is Σₕ ⌈n/2^(h+1)⌉·O(h) = O(n·Σₕ h/2^h), and Σₕ h/2^h = 2, a constant.
  4. So the total is O(n), and since every key must be read at least once it is Θ(n).

Answer: Option (D) — Θ(n).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Θ(n log n) is the cost of inserting the keys one at a time, not of the bottom-up build.
  • (B) Θ(log n) is the cost of a single MAX-HEAPIFY call.
  • (C) No comparison-based heap build is quadratic.

Common misconception. Multiplying “about n/2 calls” by “O(log n) per call” and concluding n log n. The calls are not all deep: the deepest are the fewest.

Takeaway. Bottom-up build-heap is Θ(n); repeated insertion is Θ(n log n) in the worst case.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question:
BUILD-MAX-HEAP is run on A[1..7] = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70], calling MAX-HEAPIFY on i = 3, 2, 1 in that order. A call exchanges A[i] with its larger child whenever that child is larger, and then continues from that child. How many exchanges does the complete build perform?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
BUILD-MAX-HEAP is run on A[1..7] = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70], calling MAX-HEAPIFY on i = 3, 2, 1 in that order. A call exchanges A[i] with its larger child whenever that child is larger, and then continues from that child. How many exchanges does the complete build perform?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. MAX-HEAPIFY on a node either stops immediately or performs exactly one exchange per level it descends. Counting exchanges therefore means counting the total number of levels descended by all three calls.  Step by step.  MAX-HEAPIFY(3): A[3] = 30 , children A[6] = 60 and A[7] = 70 . The larger child is 70, so 30 and 70 are exchanged (1). Index 7 is a leaf, so the call ends. Array: 10, 20, 70, 40, 50, 60, 30 . MAX-HEAPIFY(2): A[2] = 20 , children A[4] = 40 and A[5] = 50 . Exchange 20 with 50 (2). Index 5 is a leaf. Array: 10, 50, 70, 40, 20, 60, 30 . MAX-HEAPIFY(1): A[1] = 10 , children A[2] = 50 and A[3] = 70 . Exchange 10 with 70 (3). At index 3 the children are A[6] = 60 and A[7] = 30 ; exchange 10 with 60 (4). Index 6 is a leaf. Total exchanges 1 + 1 + 2 = 4, and the final array is [70, 50, 60, 40, 20, 10, 30] , which is a valid max-heap.  Answer: 4 exchanges.  Common misconception. Stopping after the first exchange at a node instead of continuing down the path, or forgetting that the key sifted to index 3 must be sifted again from there.  Takeaway. One exchange per level descended; the count is the sum of the descent depths, not the number of calls.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. MAX-HEAPIFY on a node either stops immediately or performs exactly one exchange per level it descends. Counting exchanges therefore means counting the total number of levels descended by all three calls.

Step by step.

  1. MAX-HEAPIFY(3): A[3] = 30, children A[6] = 60 and A[7] = 70. The larger child is 70, so 30 and 70 are exchanged (1). Index 7 is a leaf, so the call ends. Array: 10, 20, 70, 40, 50, 60, 30.
  2. MAX-HEAPIFY(2): A[2] = 20, children A[4] = 40 and A[5] = 50. Exchange 20 with 50 (2). Index 5 is a leaf. Array: 10, 50, 70, 40, 20, 60, 30.
  3. MAX-HEAPIFY(1): A[1] = 10, children A[2] = 50 and A[3] = 70. Exchange 10 with 70 (3). At index 3 the children are A[6] = 60 and A[7] = 30; exchange 10 with 60 (4). Index 6 is a leaf.
  4. Total exchanges 1 + 1 + 2 = 4, and the final array is [70, 50, 60, 40, 20, 10, 30], which is a valid max-heap.

Answer: 4 exchanges.

Common misconception. Stopping after the first exchange at a node instead of continuing down the path, or forgetting that the key sifted to index 3 must be sifted again from there.

Takeaway. One exchange per level descended; the count is the sum of the descent depths, not the number of calls.

questions.question: MAX-HEAPIFY(A, 2) is called on A = [16, 4, 10, 14, 7, 9, 3, 2, 8, 1]. Which array results?
questions.question_html: MAX-HEAPIFY(A, 2) is called on A = [16, 4, 10, 14, 7, 9, 3, 2, 8, 1]. Which array results?
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. MAX-HEAPIFY lets a key sink: at each step it is exchanged with the larger of its two children, and the process continues from that child until the key dominates both children or reaches a leaf.  Step by step.  At i = 2 the key is 4, with children A[4] = 14 and A[5] = 7 . The larger child is 14, so exchange: [16, 14, 10, 4, 7, 9, 3, 2, 8, 1] . The key 4 is now at i = 4, with children A[8] = 2 and A[9] = 8 . The larger child is 8, so exchange: [16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1] . The key 4 is now at i = 9, whose children A[18] and A[19] do not exist, so the call ends. Two exchanges were performed, and the subtree rooted at 2 is now a valid max-heap.  Answer: Option (A) — [16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1] .  Why the other options are wrong.  (B) stops after the first exchange and leaves 4 above 8, so the heap property still fails at index 4. (C) exchanges with 8 first, but 8 is a grandchild and is never compared at index 2. (D) moves 8 into the array while leaving 4 in place at index 2, which is not what sifting does.  Common misconception. Choosing the smaller child, or stopping as soon as the first exchange is made. MAX-HEAPIFY always picks the larger child, and it recurses.  Takeaway. A sift-down performs one exchange per level and must run to a leaf or to a point where the key already dominates its children.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. MAX-HEAPIFY lets a key sink: at each step it is exchanged with the larger of its two children, and the process continues from that child until the key dominates both children or reaches a leaf.

Step by step.

  1. At i = 2 the key is 4, with children A[4] = 14 and A[5] = 7. The larger child is 14, so exchange: [16, 14, 10, 4, 7, 9, 3, 2, 8, 1].
  2. The key 4 is now at i = 4, with children A[8] = 2 and A[9] = 8. The larger child is 8, so exchange: [16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1].
  3. The key 4 is now at i = 9, whose children A[18] and A[19] do not exist, so the call ends.
  4. Two exchanges were performed, and the subtree rooted at 2 is now a valid max-heap.

Answer: Option (A) — [16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1].

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) stops after the first exchange and leaves 4 above 8, so the heap property still fails at index 4.
  • (C) exchanges with 8 first, but 8 is a grandchild and is never compared at index 2.
  • (D) moves 8 into the array while leaving 4 in place at index 2, which is not what sifting does.

Common misconception. Choosing the smaller child, or stopping as soon as the first exchange is made. MAX-HEAPIFY always picks the larger child, and it recurses.

Takeaway. A sift-down performs one exchange per level and must run to a leaf or to a point where the key already dominates its children.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: BUILD-MAX-HEAP runs in Θ(n) time, whereas inserting the n keys one at a time costs Ω(n log n) in the worst case.
BUILD-MAX-HEAP makes exactly ⌊n/2⌋ calls to MAX-HEAPIFY.
After BUILD-MAX-HEAP the largest key is at A[1] and the second largest is at A[2] or A[3].
Building by successive insertion and building bottom-up always leave exactly the same array.
options_html: BUILD-MAX-HEAP runs in Θ(n) time, whereas inserting the n keys one at a time costs Ω(n log n) in the worst case.
BUILD-MAX-HEAP makes exactly ⌊n/2⌋ calls to MAX-HEAPIFY.
After BUILD-MAX-HEAP the largest key is at A[1] and the second largest is at A[2] or A[3].
Building by successive insertion and building bottom-up always leave exactly the same array.
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. The bottom-up build calls MAX-HEAPIFY once on every internal node, in decreasing index order, so that each subtree is already a heap when its parent is processed.  Step by step.  (A) The bottom-up build is Θ(n) by the height-sum argument. Successive insertion can force every new key to bubble up to the root, which is Ω(log n) per key and Ω(n log n) overall — attained, for instance, by inserting keys in increasing order into a max-heap. True. (B) Internal nodes are exactly 1..⌊n/2⌋ , and each is passed to MAX-HEAPIFY once. True. (C) The heap property forces the root to be the maximum. Every other key lies in one of the two subtrees of the root, so the largest of them is the larger of A[2] and A[3] . True. (D) The two procedures are both correct but not equivalent: on [1, 2, 3, 4] bottom-up gives [4, 2, 3, 1] while inserting 1, 2, 3, 4 in turn gives [4, 3, 2, 1] . False.  Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C) are correct.  Why option (D) is not selected.  A heap is not unique for a given multiset of keys. The two construction orders can leave different valid heaps, so neither can be claimed to reproduce the other.  Common misconception. Believing the O(n log n) cost of insertion forces the build to be n log n, or assuming that a correct build must be unique.  Takeaway. Bottom-up build is linear and calls MAX-HEAPIFY once per internal node; the resulting heap is valid but not unique.

  2. (B) Internal nodes are exactly 1..⌊n/2⌋, and each is passed to MAX-HEAPIFY once. True.
  3. (C) The heap property forces the root to be the maximum. Every other key lies in one of the two subtrees of the root, so the largest of them is the larger of A[2] and A[3]. True.
  4. (D) The two procedures are both correct but not equivalent: on [1, 2, 3, 4] bottom-up gives [4, 2, 3, 1] while inserting 1, 2, 3, 4 in turn gives [4, 3, 2, 1]. False.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C) are correct.

Why option (D) is not selected.

  • A heap is not unique for a given multiset of keys. The two construction orders can leave different valid heaps, so neither can be claimed to reproduce the other.

Common misconception. Believing the O(n log n) cost of insertion forces the build to be n log n, or assuming that a correct build must be unique.

questions.question:
BUILD-MIN-HEAP is run on A[1..8] = [8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1], calling MIN-HEAPIFY on i = 4, 3, 2, 1 in that order. A call exchanges A[i] with its smaller child whenever that child is smaller, and then continues from that child. How many exchanges does the complete build perform?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
BUILD-MIN-HEAP is run on A[1..8] = [8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1], calling MIN-HEAPIFY on i = 4, 3, 2, 1 in that order. A call exchanges A[i] with its smaller child whenever that child is smaller, and then continues from that child. How many exchanges does the complete build perform?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. The descending array is the worst shape for a bottom-up build: nearly every internal node has to sift its key all the way to a leaf. Count one exchange per level descended.  Step by step.  MIN-HEAPIFY(4): A[4] = 5 , single child A[8] = 1 . Exchange (1). Array [8, 7, 6, 1, 4, 3, 2, 5] . MIN-HEAPIFY(3): A[3] = 6 , children 3 and 2; smaller is 2 at index 7. Exchange (2). Index 7 is a leaf. Array [8, 7, 2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5] . MIN-HEAPIFY(2): A[2] = 7 , children 1 and 4; smaller is 1 at index 4. Exchange (3). At index 4 the single child is A[8] = 5 , smaller than 7, so exchange again (4). Array [8, 1, 2, 5, 4, 3, 6, 7] . MIN-HEAPIFY(1): A[1] = 8 , children 1 and 2; smaller is 1 at index 2. Exchange (5). At index 2 the children are 5 and 4; smaller is 4 at index 5, so exchange (6). Index 5 has no children. Final array [1, 4, 2, 5, 8, 3, 6, 7] .  Answer: 6 exchanges.  Common misconception. Assuming a descending array needs no work because it already looks “reverse ordered”. In level order it is a heap with every parent larger than its children, which for a min-heap is the maximum amount of sifting.  Takeaway. Total exchanges = sum of descent depths. A reverse-sorted array maximises it; the total stays O(n) even so.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The descending array is the worst shape for a bottom-up build: nearly every internal node has to sift its key all the way to a leaf. Count one exchange per level descended.

Step by step.

  1. MIN-HEAPIFY(4): A[4] = 5, single child A[8] = 1. Exchange (1). Array [8, 7, 6, 1, 4, 3, 2, 5].
  2. MIN-HEAPIFY(3): A[3] = 6, children 3 and 2; smaller is 2 at index 7. Exchange (2). Index 7 is a leaf. Array [8, 7, 2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5].
  3. MIN-HEAPIFY(2): A[2] = 7, children 1 and 4; smaller is 1 at index 4. Exchange (3). At index 4 the single child is A[8] = 5, smaller than 7, so exchange again (4). Array [8, 1, 2, 5, 4, 3, 6, 7].
  4. MIN-HEAPIFY(1): A[1] = 8, children 1 and 2; smaller is 1 at index 2. Exchange (5). At index 2 the children are 5 and 4; smaller is 4 at index 5, so exchange (6). Index 5 has no children. Final array [1, 4, 2, 5, 8, 3, 6, 7].

Answer: 6 exchanges.

Common misconception. Assuming a descending array needs no work because it already looks “reverse ordered”. In level order it is a heap with every parent larger than its children, which for a min-heap is the maximum amount of sifting.

Takeaway. Total exchanges = sum of descent depths. A reverse-sorted array maximises it; the total stays O(n) even so.

questions.question: In the linear-time analysis of BUILD-MAX-HEAP the work is summed over node heights as Σₕ₊₀ ⌈n/2^(h+1)⌉·O(h) = O(n·Σₕ h/2^h) = O(n). Which statement explains why this bound is linear rather than Θ(n log n)?
questions.question_html: In the linear-time analysis of BUILD-MAX-HEAP the work is summed over node heights as Σₕ₊₀ ⌈n/2^(h+1)⌉·O(h) = O(n·Σₕ h/2^h) = O(n). Which statement explains why this bound is linear rather than Θ(n log n)?
options: Only O(log n) nodes are internal, so only O(log n) calls to MAX-HEAPIFY are ever made.
Half of the nodes are leaves and do no work, a quarter descend at most one level, an eighth at most two, and so on, so Σₕ h/2^h converges to the constant 2.
Each call to MAX-HEAPIFY costs O(1) because the array is a complete binary tree.
MAX-HEAPIFY recurses at most twice at every node.
options_html: Only O(log n) nodes are internal, so only O(log n) calls to MAX-HEAPIFY are ever made.
Half of the nodes are leaves and do no work, a quarter descend at most one level, an eighth at most two, and so on, so Σₕ h/2^h converges to the constant 2.
Each call to MAX-HEAPIFY costs O(1) because the array is a complete binary tree.
MAX-HEAPIFY recurses at most twice at every node.
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. The cost of a build is dominated by where the nodes sit, not by how many there are. Nodes are numerous exactly where their height is small.  Step by step.  A complete binary tree on n nodes has ⌈n/2⌋ leaves, each of height 0 and cost 0. It has ⌈n/4⌉ nodes of height 1 costing 1 each, ⌈n/8⌉ of height 2 costing 2 each, and in general ⌈n/2^(h+1)⌉ nodes of height h costing h each. Total work is n·Σₕ h/2^(h+1) , and the series Σₕ h/2^h converges to 2, so the total is at most 2n. The few deep nodes cost log n each, but there are only a constant number of them, so their contribution is O(log n) — negligible against Θ(n).  Answer: Option (B) — the height distribution makes the sum converge to a constant.  Why the other options are wrong.  (A) There are ⌊n/2⌋ internal nodes, not O(log n). (C) A single MAX-HEAPIFY can cost O(log n); the bound is not O(1) per call. (D) MAX-HEAPIFY makes one recursive call, not two, and its depth is bounded by the height.  Common misconception. Summing the maximum cost of each call instead of weighting by how many calls have that cost. Multiplying “n/2 calls” by “log n each” ignores that only a handful of calls are deep.  Takeaway. Cost is bounded by the number of nodes at each height times that height, and that weighted sum is linear.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The cost of a build is dominated by where the nodes sit, not by how many there are. Nodes are numerous exactly where their height is small.

Step by step.

  1. A complete binary tree on n nodes has ⌈n/2⌋ leaves, each of height 0 and cost 0.
  2. It has ⌈n/4⌉ nodes of height 1 costing 1 each, ⌈n/8⌉ of height 2 costing 2 each, and in general ⌈n/2^(h+1)⌉ nodes of height h costing h each.
  3. Total work is n·Σₕ h/2^(h+1), and the series Σₕ h/2^h converges to 2, so the total is at most 2n.
  4. The few deep nodes cost log n each, but there are only a constant number of them, so their contribution is O(log n) — negligible against Θ(n).

Answer: Option (B) — the height distribution makes the sum converge to a constant.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) There are ⌊n/2⌋ internal nodes, not O(log n).
  • (C) A single MAX-HEAPIFY can cost O(log n); the bound is not O(1) per call.
  • (D) MAX-HEAPIFY makes one recursive call, not two, and its depth is bounded by the height.

Common misconception. Summing the maximum cost of each call instead of weighting by how many calls have that cost. Multiplying “n/2 calls” by “log n each” ignores that only a handful of calls are deep.

Takeaway. Cost is bounded by the number of nodes at each height times that height, and that weighted sum is linear.

questions.question: A max-heap holds 500 keys. DELETE-MAX replaces the root by the last key, shrinks the heap by one and calls MAX-HEAPIFY on the root. What is the largest number of exchanges a single DELETE-MAX can perform on this heap?
questions.question_html: A max-heap holds 500 keys. DELETE-MAX replaces the root by the last key, shrinks the heap by one and calls MAX-HEAPIFY on the root. What is the largest number of exchanges a single DELETE-MAX can perform on this heap?
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. The key moved to the root sifts down one root-to-leaf path, so the number of exchanges is bounded by the height of the tree, which is ⌊log₂ n⌋ for n nodes.  Step by step.  For n = 500, 2⁸ = 256 ≤ 500 < 512 = 2⁹ , so the height is 8: levels 0 to 8. After the deletion the heap holds 499 keys, and 2⁸ = 256 ≤ 499 < 512 , so the height is still 8. The moved key can therefore descend at most 8 edges, performing 8 exchanges. Eight exchanges are attainable: take distinct keys and make the moved key smaller than every key on one root-to-leaf path of length 8.  Answer: Option (C) — 8 exchanges.  Why the other options are wrong.  (A) 7 is the height of a heap with at most 255 keys. (B) 9 would need at least 512 keys. (D) 499 is the number of keys, not the number of levels on a path.  Common misconception. Reading “n = 500” as a height of 500, or forgetting that the heap shrinks by one before the sift-down starts.  Takeaway. DELETE-MAX costs Θ(log n): one move plus at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ exchanges.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The key moved to the root sifts down one root-to-leaf path, so the number of exchanges is bounded by the height of the tree, which is ⌊log₂ n⌋ for n nodes.

Step by step.

  1. For n = 500, 2⁸ = 256 ≤ 500 < 512 = 2⁹, so the height is 8: levels 0 to 8.
  2. After the deletion the heap holds 499 keys, and 2⁸ = 256 ≤ 499 < 512, so the height is still 8.
  3. The moved key can therefore descend at most 8 edges, performing 8 exchanges.
  4. Eight exchanges are attainable: take distinct keys and make the moved key smaller than every key on one root-to-leaf path of length 8.

Answer: Option (C) — 8 exchanges.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 7 is the height of a heap with at most 255 keys.
  • (B) 9 would need at least 512 keys.
  • (D) 499 is the number of keys, not the number of levels on a path.

Common misconception. Reading “n = 500” as a height of 500, or forgetting that the heap shrinks by one before the sift-down starts.

Takeaway. DELETE-MAX costs Θ(log n): one move plus at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ exchanges.

questions.question: HEAPSORT is implemented in place: it builds a max-heap and then repeatedly swaps A[1] with the last unsorted slot. Its worst-case running time and its auxiliary space are:
questions.question_html: HEAPSORT is implemented in place: it builds a max-heap and then repeatedly swaps A[1] with the last unsorted slot. Its worst-case running time and its auxiliary space are:
options: Θ(n log n) time and Θ(n) extra space
Θ(n²) time and Θ(1) extra space
Θ(n log n) time and Θ(1) extra space
Θ(n) time and Θ(n) extra space
options_html: Θ(n log n) time and Θ(n) extra space
Θ(n²) time and Θ(1) extra space
Θ(n log n) time and Θ(1) extra space
Θ(n) time and Θ(n) extra space
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. HEAPSORT is the only common sorting algorithm that is simultaneously Θ(n log n) in the worst case and Θ(1) in extra space.  Step by step.  The build costs Θ(n). There are n − 1 extraction steps; each swaps the root into place and sifts the new root down, costing O(log n). Total Θ(n) + (n − 1)·O(log n) = Θ(n log n) in the best, average and worst case alike. Nothing beyond a few index variables is allocated, so the extra space is Θ(1).  Answer: Option (C) — Θ(n log n) time, Θ(1) extra space.  Why the other options are wrong.  (A) Θ(n) extra space describes merge sort, not heapsort. (B) Θ(n²) describes quicksort's worst case or insertion sort, not heapsort. (D) No comparison sort of n arbitrary keys can run in Θ(n) time.  Common misconception. Assuming an in-place algorithm must be quadratic, as quicksort's worst case is. Heapsort gets both guarantees at once, which is why it is used when memory is tight and the input may be adversarial.  Takeaway. Heapsort: Θ(n log n) worst case, Θ(1) space, not stable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. HEAPSORT is the only common sorting algorithm that is simultaneously Θ(n log n) in the worst case and Θ(1) in extra space.

Step by step.

  1. The build costs Θ(n).
  2. There are n − 1 extraction steps; each swaps the root into place and sifts the new root down, costing O(log n).
  3. Total Θ(n) + (n − 1)·O(log n) = Θ(n log n) in the best, average and worst case alike.
  4. Nothing beyond a few index variables is allocated, so the extra space is Θ(1).

Answer: Option (C) — Θ(n log n) time, Θ(1) extra space.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Θ(n) extra space describes merge sort, not heapsort.
  • (B) Θ(n²) describes quicksort's worst case or insertion sort, not heapsort.
  • (D) No comparison sort of n arbitrary keys can run in Θ(n) time.

Common misconception. Assuming an in-place algorithm must be quadratic, as quicksort's worst case is. Heapsort gets both guarantees at once, which is why it is used when memory is tight and the input may be adversarial.

Takeaway. Heapsort: Θ(n log n) worst case, Θ(1) space, not stable.

questions.question:
HEAPSORT begins by running BUILD-MAX-HEAP on A[1..9] = [5, 13, 2, 25, 7, 17, 20, 8, 4]. Immediately after the build and before any extraction, what key is stored at A[3]?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
HEAPSORT begins by running BUILD-MAX-HEAP on A[1..9] = [5, 13, 2, 25, 7, 17, 20, 8, 4]. Immediately after the build and before any extraction, what key is stored at A[3]?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. The build calls MAX-HEAPIFY on i = 4, 3, 2, 1 in that order. Only after all four calls is the array a max-heap, and the question asks about that moment.  Step by step.  MAX-HEAPIFY(4): A[4] = 25 with child A[8] = 8 . 25 already dominates, so no exchange. MAX-HEAPIFY(3): A[3] = 2 with children A[6] = 17 and A[7] = 20 . Exchange 2 with 20: array becomes [5, 13, 20, 25, 7, 17, 2, 8, 4] . MAX-HEAPIFY(2): A[2] = 13 with children 25 and 7. Exchange with 25: [5, 25, 20, 13, 7, 17, 2, 8, 4] . MAX-HEAPIFY(1): A[1] = 5 with children 25 and 20. Exchange with 25 (index 2). At index 2 the children are 13 and 7, so exchange 5 with 13. Final array [25, 13, 20, 8, 7, 17, 2, 5, 4] , in which A[3] = 20 .  Answer: 20.  Common misconception. Reading A[3] from the input array (where it is 2), or stopping the build early and assuming the largest key at the root is all that matters.  Takeaway. The build must be traced to the end; the value at any interior index depends on every sift-down that passed through it.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The build calls MAX-HEAPIFY on i = 4, 3, 2, 1 in that order. Only after all four calls is the array a max-heap, and the question asks about that moment.

Step by step.

  1. MAX-HEAPIFY(4): A[4] = 25 with child A[8] = 8. 25 already dominates, so no exchange.
  2. MAX-HEAPIFY(3): A[3] = 2 with children A[6] = 17 and A[7] = 20. Exchange 2 with 20: array becomes [5, 13, 20, 25, 7, 17, 2, 8, 4].
  3. MAX-HEAPIFY(2): A[2] = 13 with children 25 and 7. Exchange with 25: [5, 25, 20, 13, 7, 17, 2, 8, 4].
  4. MAX-HEAPIFY(1): A[1] = 5 with children 25 and 20. Exchange with 25 (index 2). At index 2 the children are 13 and 7, so exchange 5 with 13. Final array [25, 13, 20, 8, 7, 17, 2, 5, 4], in which A[3] = 20.

Answer: 20.

Common misconception. Reading A[3] from the input array (where it is 2), or stopping the build early and assuming the largest key at the root is all that matters.

Takeaway. The build must be traced to the end; the value at any interior index depends on every sift-down that passed through it.
