questions.question: Which of the following statements about HEAPSORT are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about HEAPSORT are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: It is not a stable sorting algorithm.
It sorts in place, using Θ(1) auxiliary space beyond the array itself.
Building a max-heap and swapping the root into the last unsorted slot produces ascending order.
Its worst-case running time is asymptotically worse than merge sort's worst case.
options_html: It is not a stable sorting algorithm.
It sorts in place, using Θ(1) auxiliary space beyond the array itself.
Building a max-heap and swapping the root into the last unsorted slot produces ascending order.
Its worst-case running time is asymptotically worse than merge sort's worst case.
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. A max-heap keeps the largest remaining key at the root. Moving that root to the end of the unsorted prefix, then restoring the heap on the prefix, fills the array from the back with ever smaller keys.  Step by step.  (A) Sift-down moves keys over long distances, so equal keys are freely reordered. False for stability, so the statement that it is unstable is true. (B) The only extra storage is a constant number of index variables. True. (C) The largest key goes to position n, the next largest to n − 1, and so on, so the final array is non-decreasing. True. (D) Merge sort's worst case is Θ(n log n) and so is heapsort's; neither is asymptotically worse. False.  Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C) are correct.  Why option (D) is not selected.  Both algorithms are Θ(n log n) in the worst case. Heapsort is slower in practice because of cache behaviour and a larger constant factor, but that is not an asymptotic difference.  Common misconception. Confusing “in place” with “stable”, or thinking heapsort has a quadratic worst case like quicksort.  Takeaway. Heapsort: Θ(n log n) worst case, Θ(1) space, unstable, and ascending output from a max-heap.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Step by step.

  1. (A) Sift-down moves keys over long distances, so equal keys are freely reordered. False for stability, so the statement that it is unstable is true.
  2. (B) The only extra storage is a constant number of index variables. True.
  3. (C) The largest key goes to position n, the next largest to n − 1, and so on, so the final array is non-decreasing. True.
  4. (D) Merge sort's worst case is Θ(n log n) and so is heapsort's; neither is asymptotically worse. False.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C) are correct.

Why option (D) is not selected.

  • Both algorithms are Θ(n log n) in the worst case. Heapsort is slower in practice because of cache behaviour and a larger constant factor, but that is not an asymptotic difference.

Common misconception. Confusing “in place” with “stable”, or thinking heapsort has a quadratic worst case like quicksort.

Takeaway. Heapsort: Θ(n log n) worst case, Θ(1) space, unstable, and ascending output from a max-heap.

questions.question: HEAPSORT is rewritten to build a min-heap and, at every step, to swap A[1] with the last unsorted slot of the same array. The array it finally produces is:
questions.question_html: HEAPSORT is rewritten to build a min-heap and, at every step, to swap A[1] with the last unsorted slot of the same array. The array it finally produces is:
options: ascending
identical to the input array
ascending only if all keys are distinct
descending
options_html: ascending only if all keys are distinct
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. In place, the extracted extremum is parked at the back of the shrinking unsorted prefix. A min-heap extracts the smallest key first, so the smallest keys are written into the last slots first.  Step by step.  Step 1 puts the minimum at position n. Step 2 puts the second smallest at position n − 1. Continuing, the smallest key ends at the last index and the largest at index 1, which is descending order. To obtain ascending order in place, the heap must be a max-heap; a min-heap gives ascending order only when it is extracted into a separate output array.  Answer: Option (D) — descending.  Why the other options are wrong.  (A) Ascending order needs a max-heap when the extraction target is the array's tail. (B) The array is a heap at every stage and is sorted at the end, so it cannot equal an arbitrary input. (C) Distinctness is irrelevant; the direction is set by which extremum the heap exposes.  Common misconception. Assuming the heap type does not matter because both heaps “sort”. What matters is where the extracted key is written: into the array's tail, or into a separate output.  Takeaway. In place, a max-heap yields ascending order and a min-heap yields descending order; out of place, the reverse.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In place, the extracted extremum is parked at the back of the shrinking unsorted prefix. A min-heap extracts the smallest key first, so the smallest keys are written into the last slots first.

Step by step.

  1. Step 1 puts the minimum at position n.
  2. Step 2 puts the second smallest at position n − 1.
  3. Continuing, the smallest key ends at the last index and the largest at index 1, which is descending order.
  4. To obtain ascending order in place, the heap must be a max-heap; a min-heap gives ascending order only when it is extracted into a separate output array.

Answer: Option (D) — descending.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Ascending order needs a max-heap when the extraction target is the array's tail.
  • (B) The array is a heap at every stage and is sorted at the end, so it cannot equal an arbitrary input.
  • (C) Distinctness is irrelevant; the direction is set by which extremum the heap exposes.

Common misconception. Assuming the heap type does not matter because both heaps “sort”. What matters is where the extracted key is written: into the array's tail, or into a separate output.

Takeaway. In place, a max-heap yields ascending order and a min-heap yields descending order; out of place, the reverse.

questions.question: HEAPSORT and merge sort are both Θ(n log n) in the worst case, yet heapsort is usually the slower of the two on real hardware. The main reason is:
questions.question_html: HEAPSORT and merge sort are both Θ(n log n) in the worst case, yet heapsort is usually the slower of the two on real hardware. The main reason is:
options: Sift-down jumps between positions far apart in the array, so heapsort suffers many more cache misses.
Heapsort is not in place and must allocate an auxiliary array.
Heapsort's worst case is Θ(n²).
Heapsort cannot handle arrays that contain duplicate keys.
options_html: Sift-down jumps between positions far apart in the array, so heapsort suffers many more cache misses.
Heapsort is not in place and must allocate an auxiliary array.
Heapsort cannot handle arrays that contain duplicate keys.
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. Asymptotic bounds count comparisons and exchanges, not memory accesses. On a real machine the constant factor is dominated by whether those accesses hit the cache.  Step by step.  The children of index i are at 2i and 2i + 1, so a sift-down from the root touches positions n/2 apart in a single step. Each step of the descent therefore lands in a different cache line, and the first pass over a large array is essentially a random-access walk. Merge sort, by contrast, reads and writes contiguous runs, which the prefetcher handles well; quicksort's partitioning is also mostly sequential. That locality penalty, not the comparison count, is why heapsort loses in practice while remaining the better guarantee.  Answer: Option (A) — poor locality of the sift-down accesses.  Why the other options are wrong.  (B) Heapsort is the classic in-place Θ(n log n) sort; merge sort is the one that needs auxiliary space. (C) Heapsort's worst case is Θ(n log n). (D) Duplicate keys are handled correctly; heapsort is merely unstable.  Common misconception. Reading “same asymptotic bound” as “same speed”. Constants and memory behaviour decide the practical ordering.  Takeaway. Heapsort's advantage is the worst-case guarantee and Θ(1) space; its disadvantage is cache behaviour.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Asymptotic bounds count comparisons and exchanges, not memory accesses. On a real machine the constant factor is dominated by whether those accesses hit the cache.

Step by step.

  1. The children of index i are at 2i and 2i + 1, so a sift-down from the root touches positions n/2 apart in a single step.
  2. Each step of the descent therefore lands in a different cache line, and the first pass over a large array is essentially a random-access walk.
  3. Merge sort, by contrast, reads and writes contiguous runs, which the prefetcher handles well; quicksort's partitioning is also mostly sequential.
  4. That locality penalty, not the comparison count, is why heapsort loses in practice while remaining the better guarantee.

Answer: Option (A) — poor locality of the sift-down accesses.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Heapsort is the classic in-place Θ(n log n) sort; merge sort is the one that needs auxiliary space.
  • (C) Heapsort's worst case is Θ(n log n).
  • (D) Duplicate keys are handled correctly; heapsort is merely unstable.

Common misconception. Reading “same asymptotic bound” as “same speed”. Constants and memory behaviour decide the practical ordering.

Takeaway. Heapsort's advantage is the worst-case guarantee and Θ(1) space; its disadvantage is cache behaviour.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: In the standard in-place HEAPSORT, MAX-HEAPIFY is called once for each internal node during the build, and once after each of the n − 1 extraction swaps. What is the total number of MAX-HEAPIFY calls made by one complete run on n keys?
questions.question_html: In the standard in-place HEAPSORT, MAX-HEAPIFY is called once for each internal node during the build, and once after each of the n − 1 extraction swaps. What is the total number of MAX-HEAPIFY calls made by one complete run on n keys?
options: n log n
⌊n/2⌋ + n
⌊n/2⌋ + n − 1
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. Count the two phases separately. The build touches every internal node once; the extraction phase touches the root once per extraction.  Step by step.  Phase 1, the build: MAX-HEAPIFY is invoked on indices ⌊n/2⌋, …, 1 , which is ⌊n/2⌋ calls. Phase 2, extraction: for k = n down to 2, the root is swapped with position k and MAX-HEAPIFY is called on the root of the shrunken heap. That is n − 1 calls. The final extraction leaves a single element, which needs no call. Total ⌊n/2⌋ + (n − 1) calls.  Answer: Option (D) — ⌊n/2⌋ + n − 1 calls.  Why the other options are wrong.  (A) n − 1 counts only the extraction phase. (B) n log n is a bound on the work, not on the number of calls. (C) ⌊n/2⌋ + n counts one extraction too many: the last one leaves a single key and needs no sift-down.  Common misconception. Counting the calls as if the build called MAX-HEAPIFY on all n nodes. Leaves are already valid one-element heaps and are never passed to MAX-HEAPIFY.  Takeaway. Build: ⌊n/2⌋ calls. Extraction: n − 1 calls. The total is ⌊n/2⌋ + n − 1 .
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Count the two phases separately. The build touches every internal node once; the extraction phase touches the root once per extraction.

Step by step.

  1. Phase 1, the build: MAX-HEAPIFY is invoked on indices ⌊n/2⌋, …, 1, which is ⌊n/2⌋ calls.
  2. Phase 2, extraction: for k = n down to 2, the root is swapped with position k and MAX-HEAPIFY is called on the root of the shrunken heap. That is n − 1 calls.
  3. The final extraction leaves a single element, which needs no call.
  4. Total ⌊n/2⌋ + (n − 1) calls.

Answer: Option (D) — ⌊n/2⌋ + n − 1 calls.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) n − 1 counts only the extraction phase.
  • (B) n log n is a bound on the work, not on the number of calls.
  • (C) ⌊n/2⌋ + n counts one extraction too many: the last one leaves a single key and needs no sift-down.

Common misconception. Counting the calls as if the build called MAX-HEAPIFY on all n nodes. Leaves are already valid one-element heaps and are never passed to MAX-HEAPIFY.

Takeaway. Build: ⌊n/2⌋ calls. Extraction: n − 1 calls. The total is ⌊n/2⌋ + n − 1.

questions.question: A priority queue on n items must support INSERT and EXTRACT-MIN. Which representation gives the best worst-case bound for both operations together?
questions.question_html: A priority queue on n items must support INSERT and EXTRACT-MIN. Which representation gives the best worst-case bound for both operations together?
options: An unsorted array
A sorted array
A binary heap
A singly linked list kept in insertion order
options_html: A singly linked list kept in insertion order
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. The right structure is the one that keeps both operations logarithmic. Insertion into a heap costs O(log n) and extraction costs O(log n).  Step by step.  Unsorted array: INSERT is O(1) at the end, but EXTRACT-MIN needs a full scan, Θ(n). Sorted array: EXTRACT-MIN is O(1) from one end, but INSERT must shift elements, Θ(n). Binary heap: INSERT bubbles a key up one root-to-leaf path, O(log n); EXTRACT-MIN moves the last key to the root and sifts down, O(log n). Linked list in insertion order: EXTRACT-MIN is Θ(n).  Answer: Option (C) — a binary heap.  Why the other options are wrong.  (A) and (D) are linear in extraction. (B) is linear in insertion. Each of the three loses one of the two operations; only the heap keeps both logarithmic.  Common misconception. Optimising one operation in isolation. A priority queue is judged on the pair, and the workload usually mixes both.  Takeaway. Binary heap: O(log n) insert and O(log n) extract-min, with O(1) peek.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The right structure is the one that keeps both operations logarithmic. Insertion into a heap costs O(log n) and extraction costs O(log n).

Step by step.

  1. Unsorted array: INSERT is O(1) at the end, but EXTRACT-MIN needs a full scan, Θ(n).
  2. Sorted array: EXTRACT-MIN is O(1) from one end, but INSERT must shift elements, Θ(n).
  3. Binary heap: INSERT bubbles a key up one root-to-leaf path, O(log n); EXTRACT-MIN moves the last key to the root and sifts down, O(log n).
  4. Linked list in insertion order: EXTRACT-MIN is Θ(n).

Answer: Option (C) — a binary heap.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (D) are linear in extraction.
  • (B) is linear in insertion.
  • Each of the three loses one of the two operations; only the heap keeps both logarithmic.

Common misconception. Optimising one operation in isolation. A priority queue is judged on the pair, and the workload usually mixes both.

Takeaway. Binary heap: O(log n) insert and O(log n) extract-min, with O(1) peek.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Which of the following are standard uses of a priority queue? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following are standard uses of a priority queue? (Select all that apply.)
options: Huffman's algorithm, repeatedly merging the two least frequent symbols.
Prim's algorithm, repeatedly taking the cheapest edge leaving the current tree.
Binary search for a key in a sorted array.
Dijkstra's algorithm on a graph with non-negative edge weights.
options_html: Huffman's algorithm, repeatedly merging the two least frequent symbols.
Prim's algorithm, repeatedly taking the cheapest edge leaving the current tree.
Binary search for a key in a sorted array.
Dijkstra's algorithm on a graph with non-negative edge weights.
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. A priority queue is the right tool whenever the algorithm repeatedly needs the current extremum of a changing set.  Step by step.  (A) Huffman's algorithm extracts the two smallest weights, merges them and inserts the sum: two extract-mins and one insert per merge. True. (B) Prim's algorithm needs the minimum-weight crossing edge, which is exactly a decrease-key and extract-min on the frontier. True. (C) Binary search indexes the middle of a sorted array directly; it needs no ordering structure at all. False. (D) Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly extracts the unsettled vertex of least tentative distance, which is a priority-queue operation. True.  Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are correct.  Why option (C) is not selected.  Binary search relies on the array already being sorted and on random access by index. It never asks for a minimum of a dynamic set, so a priority queue would only add overhead.  Common misconception. Equating “needs ordering” with “needs a priority queue”. A priority queue is for a set whose minimum changes as elements arrive and leave.  Takeaway. Greedy algorithms that repeatedly take the best available item — Huffman, Prim, Dijkstra, A* — are the natural home of the priority queue.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A priority queue is the right tool whenever the algorithm repeatedly needs the current extremum of a changing set.

Step by step.

  1. (A) Huffman's algorithm extracts the two smallest weights, merges them and inserts the sum: two extract-mins and one insert per merge. True.
  2. (B) Prim's algorithm needs the minimum-weight crossing edge, which is exactly a decrease-key and extract-min on the frontier. True.
  3. (C) Binary search indexes the middle of a sorted array directly; it needs no ordering structure at all. False.
  4. (D) Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly extracts the unsettled vertex of least tentative distance, which is a priority-queue operation. True.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are correct.

Why option (C) is not selected.

  • Binary search relies on the array already being sorted and on random access by index. It never asks for a minimum of a dynamic set, so a priority queue would only add overhead.

Common misconception. Equating “needs ordering” with “needs a priority queue”. A priority queue is for a set whose minimum changes as elements arrive and leave.

Takeaway. Greedy algorithms that repeatedly take the best available item — Huffman, Prim, Dijkstra, A* — are the natural home of the priority queue.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: Dijkstra's algorithm is implemented with a binary heap and without a decrease-key operation: when a distance improves, a duplicate entry is pushed instead. Its running time is:
questions.question_html: Dijkstra's algorithm is implemented with a binary heap and without a decrease-key operation: when a distance improves, a duplicate entry is pushed instead. Its running time is:
options: O((V + E) log V)
O(V²)
O(V·E)
O(V log E)
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. With a binary heap the algorithm performs at most one insertion per edge relaxation and one extraction per heap entry, and each costs O(log V).  Step by step.  Each of the E edges can cause at most one successful relaxation, so at most E entries are pushed in addition to the V initial ones. The heap therefore holds O(V + E) entries, and each push or pop costs O(log(V + E)) = O(log V) because E ≤ V² and log V² = 2 log V . Total O((V + E) log V) . With decrease-key the same bound holds with fewer entries; lazy deletion only changes the constant.  Answer: Option (A) — O((V + E) log V) .  Why the other options are wrong.  (B) O(V²) is the bound for the unsorted-array or adjacency-matrix implementation. (C) O(V·E) is the bound for Bellman-Ford, which tolerates negative edges. (D) O(V log E) does not account for the E relaxations.  Common misconception. Thinking that skipping decrease-key makes the algorithm asymptotically worse. It only adds duplicate entries, and each is charged to the edge that created it.  Takeaway. Dijkstra with a binary heap is O((V + E) log V) , with or without decrease-key.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With a binary heap the algorithm performs at most one insertion per edge relaxation and one extraction per heap entry, and each costs O(log V).

Step by step.

  1. Each of the E edges can cause at most one successful relaxation, so at most E entries are pushed in addition to the V initial ones.
  2. The heap therefore holds O(V + E) entries, and each push or pop costs O(log(V + E)) = O(log V) because E ≤ V² and log V² = 2 log V.
  3. Total O((V + E) log V).
  4. With decrease-key the same bound holds with fewer entries; lazy deletion only changes the constant.

Answer: Option (A) — O((V + E) log V).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) O(V²) is the bound for the unsorted-array or adjacency-matrix implementation.
  • (C) O(V·E) is the bound for Bellman-Ford, which tolerates negative edges.
  • (D) O(V log E) does not account for the E relaxations.

Common misconception. Thinking that skipping decrease-key makes the algorithm asymptotically worse. It only adds duplicate entries, and each is charged to the edge that created it.

Takeaway. Dijkstra with a binary heap is O((V + E) log V), with or without decrease-key.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question:
Huffman coding is applied to six symbols whose frequencies are 45, 13, 12, 16, 9 and 5. What is the total number of bits in the encoded file, that is the sum over symbols of frequency × code length?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Huffman coding is applied to six symbols whose frequencies are 45, 13, 12, 16, 9 and 5. What is the total number of bits in the encoded file, that is the sum over symbols of frequency × code length?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. The total length of a Huffman-coded file equals the weighted external path length of the Huffman tree: the sum, over every merge, of the weight of the merged node.  Step by step.  Start with the six leaves 45, 16, 13, 12, 9, 5. Merge 9 and 5 into 14 (weight 14). Remaining: 45, 16, 14, 13, 12. Merge 13 and 12 into 25. Remaining: 45, 25, 16, 14. Merge 16 and 14 into 30. Remaining: 45, 30, 25. Merge 30 and 25 into 55. Remaining: 55, 45. Merge 55 and 45 into 100. The total is 14 + 25 + 30 + 55 + 100 = 224 bits, an average of 2.24 bits per symbol against 3 bits for a fixed-length code.  Answer: 224 bits.  Common misconception. Summing the code lengths of the six symbols instead of weighting each by its frequency, or forgetting that the total equals the sum of the merge weights.  Takeaway. Total Huffman cost = sum of all merge weights = weighted external path length.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The total length of a Huffman-coded file equals the weighted external path length of the Huffman tree: the sum, over every merge, of the weight of the merged node.

Step by step.

  1. Start with the six leaves 45, 16, 13, 12, 9, 5.
  2. Merge 9 and 5 into 14 (weight 14). Remaining: 45, 16, 14, 13, 12.
  3. Merge 13 and 12 into 25. Remaining: 45, 25, 16, 14.
  4. Merge 16 and 14 into 30. Remaining: 45, 30, 25.
  5. Merge 30 and 25 into 55. Remaining: 55, 45.
  6. Merge 55 and 45 into 100. The total is 14 + 25 + 30 + 55 + 100 = 224 bits, an average of 2.24 bits per symbol against 3 bits for a fixed-length code.

Answer: 224 bits.

Common misconception. Summing the code lengths of the six symbols instead of weighting each by its frequency, or forgetting that the total equals the sum of the merge weights.

Takeaway. Total Huffman cost = sum of all merge weights = weighted external path length.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: A stream of n numbers must be processed so that the 100 largest can be reported, using a heap of fixed capacity. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: A stream of n numbers must be processed so that the 100 largest can be reported, using a heap of fixed capacity. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A min-heap of capacity 100 is the right structure: its root is the smallest of the current 100 largest and is the key to evict.
A max-heap of capacity 100 works equally well.
Each arriving element costs O(log 100) time.
The total cost is O(n log 100), which is O(n) when the capacity is fixed.
options_html: A min-heap of capacity 100 is the right structure: its root is the smallest of the current 100 largest and is the key to evict.
A max-heap of capacity 100 works equally well.
Each arriving element costs O(log 100) time.
The total cost is O(n log 100), which is O(n) when the capacity is fixed.
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. To keep the k largest elements you must be able to identify, and discard, the smallest of the k you are holding. That requires the root to be the minimum, hence a min-heap.  Step by step.  (A) With a min-heap of capacity 100 the root is the weakest of the current top 100, so comparing each new element with the root and replacing it when the new element is larger keeps exactly the top 100. True. (B) A max-heap of capacity 100 exposes the largest of the stored elements, which is the last thing you would ever evict. False. (C) One comparison against the root, and at most one replacement followed by a sift-down of depth log₂ 100 ≈ 7. True. (D) n elements at O(log k) each gives O(n log k), and with k fixed at 100 this is O(n). True.  Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D) are correct.  Why option (B) is not selected.  The heap must expose the element you want to throw away, not the one you want to keep. Keeping the k largest therefore needs a min-heap of size k, just as keeping the k smallest needs a max-heap.  Common misconception. Reaching for a max-heap because the task says “largest”. The heap is chosen by which element must be evictable.  Takeaway. Top-k largest: min-heap of size k, O(n log k) time and O(k) space.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. To keep the k largest elements you must be able to identify, and discard, the smallest of the k you are holding. That requires the root to be the minimum, hence a min-heap.

Step by step.

  1. (A) With a min-heap of capacity 100 the root is the weakest of the current top 100, so comparing each new element with the root and replacing it when the new element is larger keeps exactly the top 100. True.
  2. (B) A max-heap of capacity 100 exposes the largest of the stored elements, which is the last thing you would ever evict. False.
  3. (C) One comparison against the root, and at most one replacement followed by a sift-down of depth log₂ 100 ≈ 7. True.
  4. (D) n elements at O(log k) each gives O(n log k), and with k fixed at 100 this is O(n). True.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D) are correct.

Why option (B) is not selected.

  • The heap must expose the element you want to throw away, not the one you want to keep. Keeping the k largest therefore needs a min-heap of size k, just as keeping the k smallest needs a max-heap.

Common misconception. Reaching for a max-heap because the task says “largest”. The heap is chosen by which element must be evictable.

Takeaway. Top-k largest: min-heap of size k, O(n log k) time and O(k) space.

questions.subject: programming-data-structures
questions.question: M sorted lists holding n elements in total are merged into one sorted list using a heap that holds one current element from each list. The running time is:
questions.question_html: M sorted lists holding n elements in total are merged into one sorted list using a heap that holds one current element from each list. The running time is:
options: O(n·M)
O(n log M)
O(n log n)
O(M log n)
questions.solution: Detailed solution  Concept. At any moment the next output element is the smallest of the M current heads, so a heap of size M answers each step in O(log M).  Step by step.  Initialise the heap with the first element of each non-empty list: O(M) time. Repeat n times: extract the minimum, append it to the output, and insert the next element of the list it came from. Each of the n steps costs one extract-min and at most one insert, each O(log M). Total O(n log M), which for M = 2 collapses to the linear merge of merge sort.  Answer: Option (B) — O(n log M) .  Why the other options are wrong.  (A) O(n·M) is the cost of scanning all M heads at every step. (C) O(n log n) would be right only if every element had to be compared with every other, which the heap avoids; it is also worse than O(n log M) whenever M ≪ n. (D) O(M log n) has the roles of n and M interchanged.  Common misconception. Sorting the concatenation instead of merging. Re-sorting costs O(n log n) , which ignores that the M lists are already sorted.  Takeaway. k-way merge with a heap is O(n log k) , the engine behind external sorting and multiway merge.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. At any moment the next output element is the smallest of the M current heads, so a heap of size M answers each step in O(log M).

Step by step.

  1. Initialise the heap with the first element of each non-empty list: O(M) time.
  2. Repeat n times: extract the minimum, append it to the output, and insert the next element of the list it came from.
  3. Each of the n steps costs one extract-min and at most one insert, each O(log M).
  4. Total O(n log M), which for M = 2 collapses to the linear merge of merge sort.

Answer: Option (B) — O(n log M).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) O(n·M) is the cost of scanning all M heads at every step.
  • (C) O(n log n) would be right only if every element had to be compared with every other, which the heap avoids; it is also worse than O(n log M) whenever M ≪ n.
  • (D) O(M log n) has the roles of n and M interchanged.

Common misconception. Sorting the concatenation instead of merging. Re-sorting costs O(n log n), which ignores that the M lists are already sorted.

Takeaway. k-way merge with a heap is O(n log k), the engine behind external sorting and multiway merge.
